chapters.title: Chapter 526: New World—1
paragraphs: Leon and Loriel arrived together in front of the Ascension Tower.
And there she was.
Xyra stood exactly where the portal had deposited them, her silver hair drifting without any air to move it, her deep silver eyes already fixed on the precise spot where they’d materialized.

The robe she wore made the same choices it always made about coverage, which was to say it made very few of them, the fabric doing what it could with what it had been given to work with and coming up notably short in the chest region.
Leon was not surprised she’d known they were coming. Spirit of the world — she probably knew everything that moved through it. Every person, every event, every conversation.
Including, his gut told him with unfortunate clarity, the five days on the mountain.

He considered this for a moment and then set it aside because there was genuinely nothing to be done about it, and Xyra had existed for hundreds of thousands of years. Whatever she’d witnessed, she’d witnessed considerably more in her lifetime. Ancient beings had perspective.

His spatial awareness caught something unusual about her — registered it, started to process it — and then the thought didn’t finish, because suddenly she was directly in front of him and something warm and soft pressed against his face and his entire body was locked in a grip that gave him no meaningful options.
She was hugging him.
Enthusiastically. Comprehensively. With the full physical commitment of someone who had been waiting to do this for a very long time and was not interested in doing it halfway.

He couldn’t move. Not because he lacked the strength to try, but because the differential between his strength and hers meant that trying would have been a polite academic exercise rather than an actual escape attempt.
Her voice arrived directly in his ear, bright with an excitement he’d never heard from her before.
"Leon — I have a body now. Can you believe it?"
The words landed, and his mind processed them fully, and the helplessness of his current position became considerably less relevant than what she’d just said.
A body. A physical manifestation. Which means—
Rank three.

The world had reached rank three. Not rank two with a chance of three — actually rank three, confirmed by the fact that she was currently restricting his ability to breathe at full capacity while radiating warmth through a very thin robe.

He’d known rank two was almost certain. Rank three had been the hopeful possibility, the one he’d wanted but hadn’t let himself count on. And here was the confirmation, pressed enthusiastically against him, and the excitement building in his chest was completely genuine.

"I’m so happy for you, Xyra." His voice came out slightly muffled given the circumstances, but the sincerity in it was complete. He meant it without qualification. He remembered how she’d looked when she’d first understood she had no physical body — the specific devastation of someone who had anticipated freedom for hundreds of thousands of years and received something that was freedom in shape but not in substance.
This mattered to her deeply. And he was genuinely glad.

Xyra felt his words land, and something warm moved through the new body she was still getting used to inhabiting. It wasn’t her original body — that was still sealed somewhere in the depths of the Dimensional Hourglass, preserved and inaccessible, a problem she’d solve eventually. This manifestation was different. Slightly sluggish in terms of mana control compared to what she remembered of her original capabilities, more fragile than she was accustomed to being.
She didn’t care even slightly about either of those things right now.

The physical sensation of actually holding something — of warmth transmitting through contact, of a body that responded to the world around it rather than existing slightly sideways from it — was overwhelming in the best possible way. Thousands of times better than the spirit existence she’d been in. The freedom was still incomplete, her soul still deeply connected to the world, the path to full liberation still long and unclear.

But this was now. And this was real. And the body she was pressing against had been something she’d observed for an extended period and had significant opinions about, and being the kind of ancient being she was, she didn’t particularly feel the need to be coy about any of it.
The fact that she technically couldn’t act on those opinions without certain complications didn’t stop the warmth from being very present.
After what Leon felt was a generous amount of time had passed, she finally released him.

He looked at her with an expression that landed somewhere between relief and mild helplessness. The hug had been completely non-negotiable — she’d been stronger than him before she had a body, and a physical manifestation had clearly not reduced that gap in any direction he’d have preferred.
It’s good she’s on my side,he thought simply.
On the side, Loriel had been watching all of this happen.

She’d arrived beside Leon, noticed the beautiful silver-haired woman standing in front of the tower, started forming the question of who she was — and then, without any warning or transition, the woman was simply hugging Leon with a completeness that suggested prior familiarity, and Loriel had found her lips wouldn’t open, and her voice wouldn’t come when she’d tried to say something about it.
She’d been muted. By what, she wasn’t certain. Not Leon — she was sure of that. This left only one other person present.
She could speak again now, she discovered. The effect had apparently ended on its own.
She didn’t use the voice she’d recovered.

Instead, she looked at the silver-haired woman with narrowed eyes, running a quiet assessment. The beauty was undeniable — genuinely, almost absurdly so, the kind that didn’t map cleanly onto anything Loriel had a reference for. White hair that drifted without cause. Silver eyes that held depth in a way that made regular eye contact feel like looking at something much larger than it appeared.
The hug hadn’t been the hug of someone who was Leon’s third partner. It had been something else — something with more history in it, more familiarity, a different quality entirely.
But Loriel had a bad feeling about this one anyway.

A specific, instinctive, deeply inconvenient bad feeling that she couldn’t fully articulate and wasn’t going to say out loud, because saying it out loud would require admitting she knew exactly what the feeling was.

She stood with her arms loosely at her sides and her expression carefully neutral, and watched Leon and the gorgeous ancient spirit of his world have their reunion, and the feeling stayed exactly where it was.
Third,she’d wondered when she saw the hug.
She reconsidered.
Or not third,she thought.Something else. Something worse.
She couldn’t decide which answer she preferred.
Leon didn’t mention the fact that during the hug he hadn’t been able to move at all.

He understood it clearly enough — her strength, plain and simple. The contract between them meant she couldn’t hurt him or anyone close to him, and he held full trust in that. So the inability to move had been inconvenient rather than alarming, and pointing it out felt unnecessary. She’d been waiting for a physical body for hundreds of thousands of years. She could have an enthusiastic hug.

He looked at her now — standing in front of him with that silver hair still drifting, the excitement from the hug still sitting visibly in her expression even as it settled into something calmer — and moved to what actually mattered.
"Tell me about the changes," he said. "Everything. What rank did it reach, what’s different, what opened up."
Xyra’s expression shifted into something that was both pleased and proud — the look of someone who had done something significant and was ready to explain the full scope of it.

The world had become rank three. That much he already knew from her having a body. But the details of what rank three actually meant in practice — the dungeons, the secret realms, the natural treasures, the shifts in the laws governing the space — that was what he needed to understand before he could start making decisions about what came next.
She began talking, and Leon listened with his full attention.
Loriel stood slightly to the side, watching them both, her earlier bad feeling quietly present and showing no signs of going anywhere.

chapters.title: Chapter 527: New World—2
paragraphs: Xyra launched into her explanation with the focused energy of someone who had been waiting to deliver this report and was going to do it properly.
She wasn’t trying to claim all the credit — she made that clear up front. Without the World Fragment, none of this would have been possible.

A rank three fragment feeding into an incomplete world was the foundation on which everything else had been built, and that foundation had come from Leon’s luck or fate or whatever particular quality of his existence kept producing impossible outcomes. She acknowledged that plainly.

But her credit was real too, and she wasn’t going to pretend otherwise. The merger had taken eight days instead of the predicted week. Eight days of sustained, intensive focus that had consumed her completely — no breaks, no attention to anything else happening in the world she was a part of.
She had felt everything occurring in the dimensional world during that time and had chosen not to look at any of it, which was a sacrifice that cost her more than she was going to elaborate on.
Five fucking days, she kinda regrets it.
She’d made her choice. The result was standing in front of him with a physical body, which meant the choice had been correct.

"Dungeons first." She raised one finger. "Several have formed naturally across the world. Not many — the world is new to this rank, and these things take time to settle. But they exist, drawn from the world’s own laws rather than built from the outside. Real dungeons. The kind that grow." She glanced at him. "You’ll want to map them. I know where they are."
"How large is the world now?" Leon asked.

She made a gesture that communicatedconsiderably more than beforewithout using those words. "The internal space expanded during the merger. Significantly. You’d need to explore it properly to understand the new boundaries." A slight pause. "There’s still no sun or moon. That’s a consequence of the conversion — what was a realm didn’t have an astronomical structure, and I can’t create one from nothing. But—" and here her tone became almost offhand, "—if you found a sun and moon and brought them in, integration would be straightforward."
Loriel blinked.
Leon just nodded, filing it away. He had a list of impossible things to acquire, and this was simply the newest entry on it.

"Underground formations have started." Xyra continued without waiting. "Ores, primarily. Materials that come from the world’s own substance rather than being imported — the kind that can only exist in a world mature enough to produce them. The quality will increase over time as the laws settle deeper." She tilted her head slightly. "New vegetation is spreading in regions where it didn’t exist before. And there’s a possibility — small, long timeline, nothing you’ll see soon — of native species developing. The conditions are there. Whether anything actually emerges from them is another matter."

Loriel had gone quiet in a way that was different from her usual quiet. She was processing; Leon could see it — the specific expression of someone whose framework for what was possible was being revised in real time. She’d met powerful people before. She’d treated serious illness with life element, had stood in battlefields, had trained under one of the most capable healers in the higher domain.
She’d never encountered anyone who spoke about forming a world’s ecosystem the way other people spoke about rearranging furniture.
She’s not what I thought she was,Loriel thought, watching Xyra move and speak.She’s something else entirely.
The bad feeling she’d had since arriving didn’t go away. It just settled deeper.

Leon praised Xyra when she finished — genuinely, without performance, because she deserved it completely and he wasn’t going to understate it. She received it with a particular satisfaction, the kind that came from someone who had worked extremely hard and found that the acknowledgment landed differently than expected.
Then he asked what he’d been building toward the whole time.

"The time ratio," he said. "Before the tower was integrated, this world ran at a thousand times the outside rate. It dropped to ten when the merger happened. Now that the world’s reached rank three—" He watched her face. "Is there any way to restore something closer to what it was? Even in a limited area?"
Xyra looked at him.
Her expression did something he hadn’t seen on it before — a brief, genuine confusion that had nothing to do with the question being complex and everything to do with the question being unnecessary.

She straightened slightly. Her chin lifted. "In a localized area — a couple of kilometers — adjusting time flow is not a significant undertaking." She said it with the particular weight of someone who wanted to make sure he understood this clearly. "With my involvement, it’s routine. You should have asked me this immediately."
Leon felt something release in his chest that he hadn’t realized was tight.
"Thank you," he said. "In advance. For this and for everything that’s coming after it."

He meant it fully. The slight discomfort of recognizing how much he was leaning on her capability was real — but she was standing in front of him with a physical body now, which made the dynamic feel less like borrowing from something vast and impersonal and more like a partnership between people who were building something together.
Then the last question. The one he’d been saving.
"Has a class reawakening dungeon formed here?" He kept his voice even. "Or if not — how long?"
Xyra paused mid-movement.
She went still, eyes closing briefly — not from uncertainty, but from directing her awareness inward, checking against what the world itself knew. A few seconds passed.

When her eyes opened, something moved across her face that Leon read immediately as genuine surprise. Not a small surprise. The kind that only appeared on faces that had stopped being surprised by most things a very long time ago.
"There is one forming," she said. "Right now. Not open yet. But it’s there." She refocused on him. "Ten to fifteen days."
Leon went completely still.
Then everything he’d been holding at a managed distance crashed forward at once.
Seraphine.

He’d been working toward this for longer than he wanted to calculate — the class reawakening that her potential had always deserved, the ceiling that her original class had placed on her through nothing but chance, the thing that would change everything if he could get her in front of it. He’d known for a long time that finding one was the answer. He’d also known, with equal clarity, that finding one was the hardest part.
And there was one forming naturally inside his own world, in fifteen days.

He’d need to prepare properly. Think carefully about who went in, what they brought with them, what the dungeon would demand of them. Fifteen days was enough time to do it right if he started immediately.

Xyra watched him from across the room. She’d been watching the luck accumulate around this person since she’d first become aware of him — an ascendant-rank human with a rank-three world forming naturally beneath him, a class-reawakening dungeon appearing without being sought, impossible circumstances stacking one on top of the other like the universe had decided to invest heavily in a particular outcome.
She had existed for hundreds of thousands of years.
She had never encountered anything quite like this.
She kept the thought to herself and watched his face hold the news with the expression of someone who had been hoping for something for a long time and was now standing in front of it, becoming real.

chapters.title: Chapter 528: New World—3
paragraphs: Leon was about to leave — had already formed the intention of teleporting to find Seraphine and share the news — when something pulled his attention back.

Before he could even frame the question about the dungeon location, a thread of information arrived directly in his mind. Not words exactly — an image, precise and clear, the location of the forming dungeon mapped into his awareness as if he’d been there himself. Xyra’s doing, obviously, her voice accompanying it briefly.
This is where it is.

Leon stood with the image in his mind for a moment, genuinely surprised by the delivery method. Voice transmission he could do himself — he’d copied the technique from the Kirin. But projecting a spatial image directly into someone else’s mind was different, more precise, and he filed it away as something worth learning from her later.
He turned toward her with a slight smile.
"Xyra." He meant the next part sincerely. "Thank you. For all of this. I genuinely appreciate everything you’ve done."

He meant it more completely than the words conveyed. The world fragment merger, the eight days of sustained focus, the physical manifestation she now wore, the rank three outcome, the dungeon forming — all of it connected back to her work and her capability. He’d been thinking of her as his lucky charm recently, and the thought felt accurate. Since he’d met her, things had been going remarkably well by any reasonable measure.
He glanced at Loriel to signal they were leaving.
Loriel was already gone.
He blinked at the empty space where she’d been standing, then decided she’d simply teleported back on her own, which was completely plausible, and turned to follow.
Xyra’s voice stopped him.
"You can’t just leave like this, Leon."
Something in the register was different from her usual tone — quieter, with an edge he couldn’t immediately categorize. He turned back.

"I’ve done a good job." She was looking at him steadily. "Eight days. I sacrificed eight days of complete focus. I deserve a reward, don’t I?" A pause, and her voice dropped slightly. "You don’t think I’m just a tool?"
The last question landed differently from the rest.

Leon looked at her face — the slight sadness on it, the particular quality of someone who was genuinely asking rather than performing — and felt the honest pull of someone who owed a debt and knew it.
She’s right,he thought simply.She earned something.

The problem was that he had no idea what to give her. Not from reluctance — from the genuine difficulty of identifying what would mean something to a being of her depth and age. His entire inventory, his causality reserves, his accumulated treasures — set against what she was and what she’d experienced, nothing obvious presented itself as adequate.
He was about to ask her directly — name what she wanted, and he’d provide it if he could — when she spoke again, softer, her gaze angled slightly away.
"I won’t ask for much. Don’t worry."
Then his vision blurred.

The spatial element moved around him from the outside — he recognized the signature of teleportation being applied to him rather than by him, which was a disorienting sensation. He reached instinctively for his mana and found nothing accessible. Holy energy similarly unavailable. Not blocked aggressively — simply set aside, the way you’d move something fragile out of a path, gently and without particular effort.
He didn’t fight it. The contract between them was clear. She couldn’t harm him or anyone close to him. Whatever this was, it wasn’t that.
He let himself be moved.

They arrived together in a room he’d had no awareness of existing, which itself surprised him — his spatial sense covered his entire dimensional world continuously, and he’d never detected this space. She’d built it somewhere his passive awareness hadn’t reached. Just behind the tower, he realized now, the back face of it that he’d never had cause to examine.

The room was large. Not room-sized — the part he’d arrived in was only a fraction of a considerably larger connected space that his awareness now mapped beyond the immediate walls. The color throughout was deep red: upholstery on furniture that understood what luxury meant and had no interest in moderation, paintings carrying the same color through the walls, rugs with red threading that felt like they’d been chosen by someone with very specific aesthetic convictions.
A king-sized bed occupied the center with the settled authority of furniture that had never questioned its own importance.
Xyra was seated on one of the sofas — legs crossed, posture easy, watching him with the composed directness that was simply how she looked at things.
Leon stood and took the room in. Then looked at her.
She cleared her throat.
"Just show it to me for a while," she said. "I wouldn’t mind that."
Leon’s processing paused. "Show what?"
Her voice dropped a register. Her face remained completely composed, giving away nothing about whatever was happening behind it.
"Undress."
The word arrived into the silence and sat there.
Leon went still.
I heard that correctly,he thought.That is definitely what she said.

But the distance between hearing it correctly and fully believing it was large enough that he found himself asking anyway, because the alternative was simply accepting that this was happening without verification.
"What did you say just now, Xyra?"
She made a brief sound of mild displeasure — someone who had found saying it once difficult enough and did not welcome the request for a repeat performance.
"Take off your clothes." Her tone was entirely matter-of-fact, the tone of someone explaining something self-evident to a person who should already understand it. "That’s what undress means."
Leon looked at her.
She looked back at him with the patient composure of someone who had made a request and was waiting to see what happened next.

The shock settled in fully — not the dramatic kind, not the kind that produced visible reaction, just the quiet internal variety where the mind encountered something it hadn’t prepared for and needed a moment to construct a response. He’d braced for something unusual when she’d said she had a reward in mind. His bracing had not produced this particular scenario.

He was standing in front of the most powerful being he’d ever encountered across two lifetimes of existence, in a secret red room she’d built behind his tower, and she had asked him to take his clothes off so she could look at him.
Several seconds passed.
His mouth opened.
Then closed.

He looked at the room again — at the deliberate luxury of it, the red sofa she was sitting on, the bed in the center, the space she’d clearly spent real thought constructing — and then back at her, sitting there with absolute composure, watching him process.
"You’re serious," he said.

It wasn’t really a question. He could read her well enough by now to know she wasn’t performing anything. The slight hoarseness in her voice when she’d said it the second time, the way she’d angled her gaze briefly before clarifying — those were the only signs that the request had cost her anything to make.
She was completely serious.
Xyra held his gaze and said nothing, which was itself an answer.

chapters.title: Chapter 529: The Price of a Reward
paragraphs: Leon stood frozen in the center of the red room, the weight of her words settling into him like stones dropped into still water.
Undress.

The word echoed in his skull, and for a long moment, he simply stared at her, waiting for the punchline that never came. Her silver eyes held his without wavering, without humor, without the slightest hint that this was some elaborate joke designed to test his reaction.
She was serious.
If even she’s being serious, he thought, the realization cutting through his disbelief like a blade,do I really have to strip?

The situation felt surreal. He’d walked into this room expecting something ceremonial, something symbolic, maybe a request for a rare artifact or a favor involving her ancient knowledge. Instead, he was standing in a boudoir of deep crimson while a being older than most civilizations sat watching him with the patient expectation of someone waiting for a meal to be served.
This feels so weird. So sudden.
He looked at her unblinking eyes, those silver irises that seemed to hold entire galaxies within their depths, and tried to reconcile the entity before him with the request she had just made.
Is this what she wants as her reward?
The thought circled back on itself, gaining texture and weight as he considered the implications. Had she always been like this? Had he simply failed to read her true nature from the beginning?
Was she really this lecherous from the start, and I just hadn’t known her well enough?

The idea sat uncomfortably in his chest. He respected Xyra—genuinely respected her. Her power, her precision, the way she had handled the world fragment merger with surgical care. He had begun to think of her as something approaching a partner, a companion in this strange existence he had carved out for himself.
But now, standing in her secret room with her demand hanging in the air between them, he felt the image he had constructed of her cracking at the edges.
I don’t mind doing a strip for her, he admitted to himself.Her help has been indispensable. The dungeon forming, the world fragment merging, the rank three outcome—all of it was made possible by her.

He owed her. Objectively, undeniably, he owed her, but even so, this was really out of the blue; he was also relieved that he got to know about her fetish right now, or it would be a disaster if it were in front of Seraphine and others.
But this feels so fucking weird.

He had been in situations like this before—with Seraphine, with Ira—but those had been different. Those had grown organically from connection, from mutual desire, from the slow building of intimacy over time. This was nothing like that. This was a request for payment. Transactional. Clinical.

He looked at her again, really looked at her. The way she sat on that crimson sofa, legs crossed, spine straight, her silver hair cascading over her shoulders. There was a particular quality to her posture, an authority in the way she held herself.
She gives off the vibe of a dominatrix who likes to stomp on balls.

The thought came unbidden, and Leon almost snorted despite the tension of the moment. He had no interest in that. None whatsoever. The thought of being someone’s plaything, someone’s object of domination, held zero appeal for him.
I’m not interested in that. At all.

And if her personality was such that she had done this with countless men before him—if he was just another in a long line of bodies she had summoned to this red room—that made him even less interested.
The stripping is the most I can do for her, he decided.I have nothing else to repay her with other than my body. So that’s what I’ll give. But nothing more.
He met her gaze and spoke, his voice steady despite the discomfort coiling in his gut.
"You’re serious about this?"
Xyra nodded. Not a theatrical nod. Not a hesitant one. Just a simple, direct confirmation, her silver eyes fixed on him with an intensity that made his skin prickle.

She had seen it all before. The video transmissions, the spying technique she had maintained since the beginning. She had watched him with Seraphine, with Ira, had seen every moment of intimacy he had shared in this dimensional world. But the actual thing—the real thing in front of her, alive and present—that was different.
That was the first.

Leon had no way of knowing the truth behind her composure. He couldn’t see the millennia of solitude that had shaped her, the endless years caged and isolated, watching him through her spell as the only form of entertainment in her vast and empty existence. He couldn’t know that she had never been a pervert before. That she had never desired anyone, never looked at another being with longing or lust.

Only because of those thousands of years, watching him from afar, had something shifted in her. The isolation had warped her, twisted her natural inclinations into something new. She had become a sort of pervert now, but not through nature. Through circumstance. Through the slow erosion of loneliness.

And the truth that Leon would never guess: this being, hundreds of years old, had never once held a hand with love. The only time her hands had touched another being was to crush their bones to dust. Nothing more. Nothing softer.
If Leon knew all this—if he knew the contrast between the image he had constructed of her and the reality of who she actually was—he would have been shocked.
But he didn’t know. So he accepted her confirmation with a nod of his own and reached for the clasps of his light armor.

The first piece came off easily, the material designed for quick removal in the field. He set it aside, his movements mechanical, controlled. But between each action, he paused, feeling her eyes on him.
She’s watching me like a hawk, he thought, the sensation of being observed making his skin crawl.I feel like a piece of meat laid out on a table, ready to be eaten.

He glanced at her, and sure enough, her silver gaze tracked every movement with predatory focus. She didn’t blink. She didn’t look away. She simply watched, absorbing the sight of him with an attention that bordered on unsettling.
Leon swallowed slightly and continued.

His upper garment came next, pulled over his head and dropped to the floor. His chest was bare now, the lean muscle of his torso visible, the faint scars that marked his skin catching the dim red light of the room.
Then his pants. He unfastened them, pushed them down, stepped out of them.
Now he stood in only his underwear, the final barrier between himself and complete exposure.

Xyra’s eyes dropped to that last piece of fabric, and something in her expression shifted. An intensity. A focus. She sat with one leg crossed over the other, her posture unchanged, but her silver eyes seemed to glow faintly in the dim light.
Leon felt a chill run down his spine.
She’s really focused on it, he realized.She’s actually staring at my underwear like it personally offended her.
He took a deep breath. He had already made up his mind. He had accepted that this was the price, the payment for her help. He wasn’t going to back out now.
In one smooth motion, he undid his underwear and let them fall to the floor.
He was completely naked.

The air of the room touched his skin, cool against the warmth of his body. His abs were visible, each muscle defined, the lines of his torso carving a path downward. Below that, his cock hung soft and limp between his legs, not hard, not aroused.
Even in its relaxed state, it was substantial. When erect, it became a ten-inch monster—veiny, thick, and demanding. Seraphine and Ira could both attest to that.

His body was lean and chiseled, the product of a lifetime of combat (even if the lifetime in question had been separated into two segments by death). His face was extremely handsome, sharp and angular, framed by long silver-white hair that fell past his shoulders.
A detail that he shared with Xyra. They both had the same silver-white hair.
There, Leon thought, preparing to speak.You’ve seen what you wanted. Can I get dressed now?
But before he could utter a single word, before he could even form the sentence on his tongue, something changed.

Definitely an elf.
He remembers seeing her last time, but he was in too much of a hurry before.
And she was looking directly at him.
There was a gleam in her eyes.
A sheen of interest, of recognition, of something that made his instincts scream warning.
The first thought that entered Leon’s mind when seeing that gorgeous beauty was simple:Leave.
These too-beautiful women were trouble.
He had just had a whole new experience with one before coming here.
His balls were still empty, his cock still sensitive, his mind still reeling from the ancient silver-haired goddess who had sucked him dry five times.
He did not need another encounter.
Not tonight.
Not ever, if he could help it.
Even without talking to her, his assumptions made it clear it was going to be trouble if he decided to engage with her.
The way she was looking at him—like she wanted him to come over, to speak, to give her an excuse to interact—set off every alarm in his head.
Her role sitting there spoke for itself.
She seemed to be staff, like a receptionist, probably there to resolve any questions he might have.
But right now, Leon could not be bothered.
His strides never stopped for even a second.

chapters.title: Chapter 536: A Reward Beyond Expectations—5
paragraphs: He scanned the room quickly, his eyes catching the various symbols and signs posted around the walls. Directional markers. Floor guides. He spotted the indicators for Floor 1 and Floor 2, thanked the designers for their clear signage, and adjusted his path accordingly. He moved through the lounge with purposeful steps, weaving past furniture and decorative pillars, his gaze fixed ahead.
He felt the elf’s golden eyes on his back the entire time.
He did not look back.
He quickly found his way through different corridors, following the signs until he arrived at a white portal set into the wall. Above it, written in elegant script, were the words: Floor 2.
Relief washed over him. He had made it without having to engage in conversation.
Before stepping through the portal, he stopped.

He reached into his inventory and took out a handful of round objects. They had a slight darkish hue to them, pulsing faintly with corrupted energy. There were a little more than fifty of them in total. All of them were corrupted cores. And all of them were from Archon-ranked beasts—the ones he had collected right after the battle in the dimensional merger zone.

The other beasts’ cores were not important enough to prioritize. They were still being harvested by his people, processed through the normal channels. But these Archon-grade cores were different. They were valuable. Powerful. And he needed them.

The upcoming Class Reawakening Dungeon participants—the people he considered like family—wouldn’t benefit from these cores. In the dungeon, level and cultivation rank wouldn’t matter. Everyone would be plummeted to level 1, stripped of their power, and forced to start from scratch. These cores would be wasted on them.
So Leon could use them all for himself.

Not only that, he still hadn’t checked his stats since he had cleared the first floor of the tower. He had been too busy with the dimensional merger, with Xyra’s arrival, with the chaos of everything that had happened. His progress had been recorded but not reviewed. His strength had increased but was not fully accounted for.
Before entering the second floor, he needed to be ready. Completely ready.

He sat down cross-legged on the floor, arranging the cores in a neat circle around him. The dark energy seeped from them, staining the air with a malevolent hum. Fifty-three Archon-grade cores. A fortune in power. A feast of corruption that would fuel his ascension.
He began the purification.

His holy energy surged from his core, the pure white light that was the nemesis of the abyssal corruption. It flowed through his hands into the first core. The dark hue resisted, writhing against the light like a living thing. But Leon’s energy was relentless. It burned through the corruption, layer by layer, dissolving the abyssal taint until only pure, refined mana remained.
The first core turned clear, its dark hue replaced by a soft, radiant glow.
Leon set it aside and reached for the next.

One by one, he purified the cores. His holy energy worked methodically, efficiently, burning through the corruption with the precision of a surgeon. Sweat beaded on his forehead. His breathing grew heavier. But he did not stop.
Fifty-three cores.

Each one took several minutes of focused, sustained effort. The total time stretched into hours. The corridor was silent except for the hum of his energy and the faint crackle of dissolving corruption.
The elf receptionist did not disturb him. Perhaps she sensed his focus. Perhaps she was waiting for another time.
Either way, Leon was grateful.
The purification continued.

Leon sat cross-legged on the cold stone floor of the corridor, the fifty-three Archon-grade corrupted cores arranged in a rough pile before him. The faint hum of abyssal energy vibrated through the air, a dark chorus that would have made lesser men tremble. But Leon’s expression was calm, his breathing steady, his focus absolute.
He reached down and picked up the first core.

His holy energy ignited in his palm, pure white light surging from his core and flooding the corrupted stone. The reaction was immediate. The dark hue writhed, black smoke hissing as it tried to escape the purifying touch. But Leon’s energy was relentless. It burned through the corruption layer by layer, dissolving the abyssal taint with surgical precision.
Five minutes.
The core turned clear, its dark hue replaced by a soft, radiant glow. Then, in a quiet sigh of light, it crumbled to ash in his palm.
Leon let the ash fall through his fingers and reached for the next one.
Five minutes.
Another core purified. Another handful of ash.

The process was methodical. Meditative. Each core required exactly that amount of time—no more, no less. The purification was a steady burn, consistent and efficient. Leon settled into the rhythm, his breathing syncing with the flow of his holy energy, his mind emptying of everything except the task before him.
Twenty minutes passed. Four cores done.
An hour. Twelve cores done.
Two hours. Twenty-four cores.

Leon did not stop. He did not rest. The pile of ash beside him grew, a soft gray mound that shifted with the faint breeze from the corridor. His holy energy flowed without pause, a continuous stream of purification that showed no signs of wavering.
Three hours. Thirty-six cores.
Four hours. Forty-eight cores.
Five minutes for the forty-ninth. Five for the fiftieth. Five for the fifty-first.
Five minutes for the fifty-second.

Leon reached for the fifty-third and final core. It was the largest of them all, pulsing with a deep, malevolent darkness that seemed to resist even before he touched it. The Archon beast that had yielded this core had been the strongest of the group. The corruption was denser, more concentrated, more stubborn.
He pressed his palm against it and released his holy energy.
The darkness fought back.

Black tendrils surged out, wrapping around his wrist, trying to sink into his skin. Leon gritted his teeth and pushed harder. His light flared, burning brighter, hotter, more intense. The tendrils screamed—a silent vibration that echoed in his skull—and retreated.
Five minutes.
The final core turned clear, pulsed once, and crumbled to ash.
Leon let out a long, slow breath.
Fifty-three Archon-grade cores, all purified. All turned to ash.

He looked at the gray mound beside him, then at his empty palms. The power that had once been locked inside those cores now floated freely in the air around him, waiting to be absorbed. He closed his eyes, centered his breathing, and began.
He pulled the ambient mana into his core.

It came willingly, the purified energy recognizing his affinity, flowing into his meridians like water finding its level. Leon guided it through his channels, nourishing his foundation, reinforcing his base. His level stirred.
Level 46. The first threshold is approached.
He gathered more energy, compressing it, refining it through his core. The barrier between 46 and 47 was thin, weakened by his previous training. The purified mana surged, pushed, and broke through.
Level 47.
Leon kept going. The ambient mana was rich, dense, more than enough to fuel his continued ascent. He pulled it in waves, each surge carrying him closer to the next threshold.
Level 48.
His body hummed. His meridians stretched, accommodating the influx. The energy was pure, refined, perfectly compatible with his cultivation. There was no resistance, no friction. Only growth.
Level 49.

He was approaching the peak of the Ascendant rank. The barrier between 49 and 50 was thicker, more substantial. It required more pressure, more energy, and more focus to break. But Leon had fifty-three Archon-grade cores’ worth of mana to draw from. He had more than enough.
He gathered his power, centered his intent, and pushed.
The barrier cracked. Splintered. Shattered.
Level 50.

Power exploded through him, a surge of energy that made his whole body tremble. His senses sharpened, his perception expanding as the next rank settled into place. He could feel the difference immediately—stronger channels, denser mana, a deeper connection to the world around him.
Leon opened his eyes.
He had reached level 50.

The edge of the Ascendant rank. One more level, and he would ascend to Sage. That was enormous. A breakthrough that would redefine his capabilities, unlock new changes, and probably elevate his combat power to a whole new tier.

But that final step would require more than just energy. It required insight. Enlightenment. A moment of understanding that could not be forced through raw mana alone, and it was not like he had enough mana core to force his way.
He would reach it. Soon.
For now, level 50 was enough.
Leon looked at the pile of ash, then at his hands. He felt the new power coursing through him, the familiar hum of a recent breakthrough settling into his bones.
He stood, stretching his limbs. His body felt lighter, more responsive. The fatigue from the purification process had faded, replaced by the invigorating sensation of newfound strength.
The corridor was silent. The white portal to Floor 2 still glowed ahead of him, waiting.
Leon didn’t take a step forward; instead, he called out status in his mind as a golden translucent window appeared in front of his eyes.

chapters.title: Chapter 537: Second Floor of the Ascension Tower
paragraphs: Leon finished purifying the last of the fifty-three cores and absorbed it, feeling the final addition register cleanly before he opened his status screen.
The numbers appeared in front of him, and he read through them without rushing, taking each section properly rather than skimming.
He started at the top.
[Name: Prim Leo’el Divaneth]
[Level: 50]
[Class: Elemental Paragon (SSS)]
[Age: 19 (Soul Age: 35)]
[Race: Divinordial (Could not be measured)]
[Titles: Hope Breaker (Common), Path Forger (Epic), World Keeper (Legendary), Creator (Mythic), Myth Breaker (Mythical), Anomaly (Divine)]
[Cultivation: Ascendant Rank]
[Affinity: All (Rank 7)]
[Strength: ★★★]
[Agility: ★★★]
[Stamina: ★★★]
[Intelligence: 15,120]
[Skills:]
– Elemental Surge (Legendary– Level 100)...
[Techniques:]
– Mana Body Enhancement (Common – Transcendent Rank)...
[Concepts:]
– Lightning Aura (Level 4)...
Level fifty. Higher than his rough estimate — the other nothing using those archon-ranked cores had only made this possible, and everything since had stacked more than he’d been tracking. Good.
He moved past class and age without pause. Elemental Paragon SSS, nineteen outside and thirty-five inside — nothing he needed to revisit.

Cultivation: Ascendant. Still. He’d known it would be. Realm advancement wasn’t something combat experience produced on its own — it required a qualitative shift beyond the raw cores rather than accumulated quantity. He could feel the ceiling clearly enough. Not today’s problem.

Affinity: All, Rank 7. He let that land properly for a moment. Every element at that level, passively, all the time. The gap between rank six and rank seven had been significant in practice. He appreciated seeing it again; that was only before the elemental surge.
Then the titles.
[Titles: Hope Breaker (Common), Path Forger (Epic), World Keeper (Legendary), Creator (Mythic), Myth Breaker (Mythical), Anomaly (Divine)]
He skimmed Hope Breaker, Myth Breaker, and Anomaly without stopping — all three were familiar, nothing new in them worth dwelling on. He kept moving.
Path Forger caught his attention properly for the first time in a while.

[Path Forger (Epic)]You break established progression constraints. Grants permanent immunity to environmental restrictions, structural locks, and standard scaling limitations, allowing you to bypass forced progression rules.

He’d felt this working without always recognizing it as this specifically — the way certain barriers that should have applied to him simply hadn’t. Domain restrictions, cultivation ceilings, the invisible architecture that the Upper Ones had built into the world’s structure. Path Forger was why those things bent around him rather than stopping him. Useful to have it confirmed in writing.
World Keeper next.

[World Keeper (Legendary)]You possess absolute ownership, spatial awareness, and authority over a bound ecosystem or realm. Allows you to freely manipulate environmental laws, access points, and spatial boundaries of any space under your direct stewardship.

This one he understood intimately. Everything he did inside his dimensional world — the teleportation without mana cost, the absolute control over what moved and where, the ability to lock the ancient entity in place simply by being the master of the space — was all World Keeper. The title wasn’t abstract. It was the mechanism behind half of what had kept him alive in the hardest moments, and he could do the same thing to any space he had ownership of.
This title was simply absurd, while the thing that had given this ability was definitely not overpowered; this was overpowered, to say the least, in certain circumstances.
The creator came after it.

[Creator (Mythic)]Grants the conceptual authority to weave raw world-laws. You can accelerate the generation of natural resources, manifest unique biomes, or establish fundamental systemic rules within a space bound to your authority.
He read this one slowly.
Accelerate the generation of natural resources. Establish fundamental systemic rules.

He hadn’t used this consciously. He’d been operating through Xyra for the world’s development — letting her handle the merger, the law formation, the structural changes that came with ranking up. But the title suggested he had his own access to that layer of authority, independent of her. Not at her level. Not with her expertise or her hundreds of thousands of years of understanding. But present.
Something to explore when he had time.
Physical stats next, and they were exactly what he’d expected.
[Strength: ★★★]
[Agility: ★★★]
[Stamina: ★★★]

Three stars across all three. Perfectly even — the Divinordial physiology elevated everything simultaneously rather than favoring one category. He didn’t need to think too hard about what three stars in all three categories translated to in real terms. He’d felt it in practice. The mathematics got uncomfortable quickly.
Then the two that actually made him stop.
[Intelligence: 15,120]
He read the mana number twice.

Thirty-two thousand. His rough working estimate had been sitting around twenty thousand, maybe slightly above. The gap between that estimate and the actual figure was large — large enough that he’d clearly been significantly undervaluing what the continuous accumulation had produced over time.
The intelligence number hit differently.
Fifteen thousand, one hundred and twenty.

He hadn’t anticipated that. He’d known it was high — the processing speed, the multicasting capability, the Leximancy scaling — but fifteen thousand gave all of it a precise context. It explained why complex spatial calculations resolved almost automatically under pressure, why his tactical reading of situations felt instinctive rather than deliberate. The number wasn’t just high. It was working.
He moved to the dual-heart section.
[Dual-Heart Physiology]

The original human heart turned Divinordial core remains completely intact, but beside it formed a second heart entirely made from the dark crystalline energy of the universe. It appeared black at first glance, yet faint silver patterns resembling galaxies moved beneath its surface. Tiny cracks of violet light pulsed across it like veins. Unlike a normal heartbeat, the Void Heart pulsed slowly and heavily. Every pulse distorted nearby mana slightly.
He put his hand against his chest.

Both of them, distinct and present. The original heart, steady and strong, was the familiar rhythm he’d had since this body became his. The Void Heart beneath it — slower, heavier, each pulse carrying a different weight entirely. The mana distortion it generated was something he’d stopped consciously noticing because it was constant. Focusing on it now, he could feel the subtle field around each beat, the way nearby energy bent slightly in response.
One thing struck him that hadn’t struck him before.

The race line still said Divinordial. Singular. No modification, no additional classification for the second heart, no system notation acknowledging that what was sitting in his chest was two physiologically distinct things operating simultaneously.
The system saw the whole arrangement as one thing.
It doesn’t separate them,he thought.Whatever the Void Heart is, the system has absorbed it into the Divinordial classification rather than treating it as a separate element for now.
That was either reassuring or concerning, and he couldn’t immediately decide which. He filed it and kept reading.
[Primordial Void Heart]
Rank: ???
Type: Unique Constitution
[Void Assimilation]
The heart automatically absorbs traces of surrounding foreign energy. Instead of corrupting him, the heart refines him, forcing continuous internal evolution.
[Mana Purification]
His mana becomes denser and purer than normal mana. Spells are fundamentally denser, more destructive, and cleanly overwhelm standard mana versions at a fraction of the cost.
[Dimensional Resistance]
The Void Heart stabilizes his existence. Grants resistance to spatial crushing, illusion worlds, dimensional storms, and better survival on higher floors.
[Evolution Catalyst]
The Void Heart reacts to powerful energies and slowly evolves. The heart itself can rank up later, unlock hidden abilities, mutate skills, or awaken new traits.
[Hidden Trait — Void Devouring]
When near death, the heart forcibly absorbs nearby energy to keep the host alive, devouring enemy mana, dungeon energy, or remnants of dead monsters. Highly volatile.

First and foremost, Leon remembers the heart rank being Epic before it merged with him; however, it had become just a question mark. It seems that, through the stimulation of his other heart, it might have already evolved a bit, or the question mark could be because of his still being primordial with this unknown heart, which he doesn’t know fully yet.

Void Assimilation explained the mana number immediately. Every battle, every environment saturated with abyssal or elemental energy, every encounter with corrupted beasts — all of it was automatically processed and refined while he focused on other things. He hadn’t been doing anything deliberate. It had simply been running continuously since the heart formed.
That’s where the extra twelve thousand came from,he thought.

Mana Purification he understood before he’d had language for it — the consistent way his attacks outperformed their cost, the way opponents’ defenses yielded faster than his raw output justified. The mechanism was clearer now.

Dimensional Resistance explained the tower’s first floor more cleanly than he’d been able to at the time. Certain sections had felt dangerous in a way that hadn’t fully materialized into actual danger. The heart stabilizing his existence had been the reason.
The rank showing as exceeding classification authority, he found quietly amusing. The tower couldn’t measure it. He filed that in the column of problems he was comfortable having.
He read Void Devouring twice and took it seriously.

He’d felt it during the worst moments of the dimensional world fight — the pulling sensation when the injuries were most severe, the heart working harder. Now he had the confirmation that it was real and intentional.
Highly volatile.
A survival mechanism that triggered automatically was useful. One that was volatile meant it might do something unpredictable in the process of keeping him alive. Worth not treating as a plan.
He closed the screen and stood quietly for a moment.
Stronger than he’d been giving himself credit for. Gaps are still real and present. The path forward is clearer than it had been before reading any of this.
Leon was more than satisfied with his change, and just by knowing it all, he felt even more confident than before.
He stepped through the second-floor portal with a calmness on his face.

[World Keeper (Legendary)]You possess absolute ownership, spatial awareness, and authority over a bound ecosystem or realm.
Allows you to freely manipulate environmental laws, access points, and spatial boundaries of any space under your direct stewardship.
This one he understood intimately.

Everything he did inside his dimensional world — the teleportation without mana cost, the absolute control over what moved and where, the ability to lock the ancient entity in place simply by being the master of the space — was all World Keeper.
The title wasn’t abstract.
It was the mechanism behind half of what had kept him alive in the hardest moments, and he could do the same thing to any space he had ownership of.
This title was simply absurd, while the thing that had given this ability was definitely not overpowered; this was overpowered, to say the least, in certain circumstances.
The creator came after it.
[Creator (Mythic)]Grants the conceptual authority to weave raw world-laws.
You can accelerate the generation of natural resources, manifest unique biomes, or establish fundamental systemic rules within a space bound to your authority.
He read this one slowly.
Accelerate the generation of natural resources.
Establish fundamental systemic rules.
He hadn’t used this consciously.
He’d been operating through Xyra for the world’s development — letting her handle the merger, the law formation, the structural changes that came with ranking up.
But the title suggested he had his own access to that layer of authority, independent of her.
Not at her level.
Not with her expertise or her hundreds of thousands of years of understanding.
But present.
Something to explore when he had time.
Physical stats next, and they were exactly what he’d expected.
[Strength: ★★★]
[Agility: ★★★]
[Stamina: ★★★]
Three stars across all three.
Perfectly even — the Divinordial physiology elevated everything simultaneously rather than favoring one category.
He didn’t need to think too hard about what three stars in all three categories translated to in real terms.
He’d felt it in practice.
The mathematics got uncomfortable quickly.
Then the two that actually made him stop.
[Intelligence: 15,120]
He read the mana number twice.
Thirty-two thousand.
His rough working estimate had been sitting around twenty thousand, maybe slightly above.
The gap between that estimate and the actual figure was large — large enough that he’d clearly been significantly undervaluing what the continuous accumulation had produced over time.
The intelligence number hit differently.
Fifteen thousand, one hundred and twenty.
He hadn’t anticipated that.
He’d known it was high — the processing speed, the multicasting capability, the Leximancy scaling — but fifteen thousand gave all of it a precise context.
It explained why complex spatial calculations resolved almost automatically under pressure, why his tactical reading of situations felt instinctive rather than deliberate.
The number wasn’t just high.
It was working.
He moved to the dual-heart section.
[Dual-Heart Physiology]
The original human heart turned Divinordial core remains completely intact, but beside it formed a second heart entirely made from the dark crystalline energy of the universe.
It appeared black at first glance, yet faint silver patterns resembling galaxies moved beneath its surface.
Tiny cracks of violet light pulsed across it like veins.
Unlike a normal heartbeat, the Void Heart pulsed slowly and heavily.
Every pulse distorted nearby mana slightly.
He put his hand against his chest.
Both of them, distinct and present.
The original heart, steady and strong, was the familiar rhythm he’d had since this body became his.
The Void Heart beneath it — slower, heavier, each pulse carrying a different weight entirely.
The mana distortion it generated was something he’d stopped consciously noticing because it was constant.
Focusing on it now, he could feel the subtle field around each beat, the way nearby energy bent slightly in response.
One thing struck him that hadn’t struck him before.
The race line still said Divinordial.
Singular.

No modification, no additional classification for the second heart, no system notation acknowledging that what was sitting in his chest was two physiologically distinct things operating simultaneously.
The system saw the whole arrangement as one thing.
It doesn’t separate them,he thought.Whatever the Void Heart is, the system has absorbed it into the Divinordial classification rather than treating it as a separate element for now.
That was either reassuring or concerning, and he couldn’t immediately decide which.
He filed it and kept reading.
[Primordial Void Heart]
Rank: ???
Type: Unique Constitution
[Void Assimilation]
The heart automatically absorbs traces of surrounding foreign energy.
Instead of corrupting him, the heart refines him, forcing continuous internal evolution.
[Mana Purification]
His mana becomes denser and purer than normal mana.
Spells are fundamentally denser, more destructive, and cleanly overwhelm standard mana versions at a fraction of the cost.
[Dimensional Resistance]
The Void Heart stabilizes his existence.
Grants resistance to spatial crushing, illusion worlds, dimensional storms, and better survival on higher floors.
[Evolution Catalyst]
The Void Heart reacts to powerful energies and slowly evolves.
The heart itself can rank up later, unlock hidden abilities, mutate skills, or awaken new traits.
[Hidden Trait — Void Devouring]
When near death, the heart forcibly absorbs nearby energy to keep the host alive, devouring enemy mana, dungeon energy, or remnants of dead monsters.
Highly volatile.
First and foremost, Leon remembers the heart rank being Epic before it merged with him; however, it had become just a question mark.

It seems that, through the stimulation of his other heart, it might have already evolved a bit, or the question mark could be because of his still being primordial with this unknown heart, which he doesn’t know fully yet.
Void Assimilation explained the mana number immediately.
Every battle, every environment saturated with abyssal or elemental energy, every encounter with corrupted beasts — all of it was automatically processed and refined while he focused on other things.
He hadn’t been doing anything deliberate.
It had simply been running continuously since the heart formed.
That’s where the extra twelve thousand came from,he thought.
Mana Purification he understood before he’d had language for it — the consistent way his attacks outperformed their cost, the way opponents’ defenses yielded faster than his raw output justified.
The mechanism was clearer now.
Dimensional Resistance explained the tower’s first floor more cleanly than he’d been able to at the time.
Certain sections had felt dangerous in a way that hadn’t fully materialized into actual danger.
The heart stabilizing his existence had been the reason.
The rank showing as exceeding classification authority, he found quietly amusing.
The tower couldn’t measure it.
He filed that in the column of problems he was comfortable having.
He read Void Devouring twice and took it seriously.
He’d felt it during the worst moments of the dimensional world fight — the pulling sensation when the injuries were most severe, the heart working harder.
Now he had the confirmation that it was real and intentional.
Highly volatile.
A survival mechanism that triggered automatically was useful.
One that was volatile meant it might do something unpredictable in the process of keeping him alive.
Worth not treating as a plan.
He closed the screen and stood quietly for a moment.
Stronger than he’d been giving himself credit for.
Gaps are still real and present.
The path forward is clearer than it had been before reading any of this.
Leon was more than satisfied with his change, and just by knowing it all, he felt even more confident than before.
He stepped through the second-floor portal with a calmness on his face.

chapters.title: Chapter 538: Second Floor of the Ascension Tower—1
paragraphs: Leon stepped through the portal.
The space on the other side wasn’t what he’d expected.

The first floor had announced itself immediately — grand, deliberate, the architecture of something built to impress before it began killing you. This was different. The portal deposited him onto a narrow stone platform suspended in open air, and beyond the platform’s edges there was simply nothing. No floor, no ceiling, no walls he could see. Just dark space extending in every direction, and hanging within that darkness, at varying distances and heights, hundreds of stone platforms exactly like the one he was standing on.
They were connected by nothing. No bridges, no paths, no obvious route between them.

Each platform had something on it. From where he stood he could make out shapes — some held objects, some held what appeared to be constructs or mechanisms, a few held things that were moving. The platforms themselves varied in size from barely large enough to stand on to broad expanses the size of small courtyards.
No overseer appeared. No voice explained the rules.
Leon stood on his platform and took it all in for a full thirty seconds, his spatial awareness expanding outward to map what he was working with.
Right,he thought.Figure it out yourself.

His awareness gave him the dimensions of the space — enormous, far larger than the first floor had been, the darkness extending further than his range could fully cover. He counted the platforms within range: two hundred and fourteen, arranged without obvious pattern, spread across three dimensions rather than just horizontal space. Some were above him, some below, some at angles that made no gravitational sense.

Several of the moving things on distant platforms noticed him at the same moment his awareness touched them. He felt them orient in his direction with the specific quality of things that had been waiting for something to arrive.
Immediate problem,he noted without urgency.

He looked at the platform nearest to him — about fifteen meters away, slightly below his current position. It held a stone pedestal with something resting on top of it. Too far to read clearly even with his enhanced vision, which told him whatever it was had some kind of visual obscuration on it.

The second nearest platform was larger, roughly twenty meters away and at the same height. It held one of the moving constructs — humanoid in shape, standing still now but clearly aware of him, its head tracking his position.
He made a decision and teleported to the platform with the pedestal.

The construct on the adjacent platform moved the instant he did — not toward him, but repositioning, the movement precise and considered. It wasn’t charging. It was adjusting to his new position with the measured response of something that was tracking rather than attacking.
It’s watching,Leon thought.Not attacking yet. There’s a condition.

He looked at the pedestal. The object resting on it was a flat disc of dark stone, roughly the size of his palm, covered in runes he didn’t immediately recognize. Not the basic runes he’d been studying since acquiring the Rune Scriber’s kit. These were different — older in feel, more compressed, each symbol doing more work than the ones he’d learned.
He didn’t touch it. Not yet.

He extended his awareness across it carefully instead, reading the energy structure the way he’d learned to read corrupted cores — looking for the shape of what it was doing rather than trying to force it open.

The disc was a key. That was the closest analogy he could construct. It held a pattern that corresponded to something else in this space, a lock somewhere among the two hundred and fourteen platforms that this specific configuration of runes would open or activate. Touching it without understanding the pattern would — his awareness caught the secondary layer of the object — trigger something he didn’t want triggered.
He filed the disc as not yet and turned to look at the construct that was still watching him from the adjacent platform.
It was waiting for him to make a mistake with the disc. That was his read of it. Touch it wrong and the construct engaged. Navigate it correctly and something else happened.
He looked across the space at the other platforms within visible range, trying to find the one that corresponded to this disc.

He spotted it after about forty seconds — a platform roughly sixty meters away and twenty meters below his current position, larger than most of the others, with a circular depression in its center that matched the disc’s dimensions exactly. The rune pattern around the depression’s edge corresponded to the disc’s surface pattern in a way that confirmed the relationship.
The problem was the space between here and there.
Teleportation was the obvious solution. He could teleport to that platform directly and deal with whatever was there.

But he spent another ten seconds just watching the space instead of moving, because the first floor had taught him that the obvious solution in this tower was usually a test of whether you’d noticed the non-obvious element first.
He found it on the eleventh second.

Between his current position and the target platform, three of the intervening platforms held constructs similar to the one already watching him. All three were oriented toward the direct path between the two points, positioned at angles that suggested they’d been placed specifically to cover that route.

They weren’t blocking it in a way that made the teleportation impossible. They were covering the approach in a way that made a blind teleport directly to the target dangerous — he’d arrive on the target platform with three constructs already responding to his movement, in positions that gave them immediate angles on him.
They want me to take the obvious line,he thought.And they’ve stacked the obvious line.

He looked for a different route. Not direct — angled, using platforms the constructs weren’t covering, accepting a longer path in exchange for arriving at the target without three things already oriented toward him.
He found one. Four platform hops instead of one direct jump, angling below and around the construct coverage zone before coming up to the target from a direction none of the three were watching.

He pocketed the disc — carefully, with his awareness fully engaged on its secondary trigger layer, making sure the act of taking it didn’t activate anything. It didn’t. The trigger was contact with the disc’s face in a specific way, not simply taking it.
Then he moved.
First hop: platform thirty meters to his left and slightly below.
FWOOSH.
The three constructs tracking his previous position adjusted. Not fast — deliberately, methodically, the movement of something recalculating rather than reacting.
Second hop: another platform, dropping further below the construct coverage zone.
FWOOSH.
Third hop: angling back upward, coming around the far side of the space.
Fourth hop: the target platform, arriving from below and behind the angle any of the constructs had been watching.
He landed clean, the disc in his hand, the circular depression directly in front of him.
He pressed the disc into the depression and felt the rune patterns align.
The platform shuddered. From somewhere in the darkness above, a section of the space shifted — platforms moving, a configuration changing, something new becoming accessible that hadn’t been before.
And from the adjacent platform, the construct that had been watching him since he arrived finally moved toward him with purpose.
Condition met,Leon thought, his sword already in his hand.Now it engages.

chapters.title: Chapter 539: Second Floor of the Ascension Tower—2
paragraphs: The construct crossed the gap between platforms in two steps and swung.
Leon ducked under it, the strike passing close enough that he felt the displaced air against the top of his head, and came back up with his sword already moving.
CLANG!

The blade connected with the construct’s forearm and the impact told him several things at once. Dense. Not stone despite looking like it — the internal structure was something harder, more uniform, without the grain or fracture points that stone had. His sword had moved it but hadn’t damaged it.
Not a material I can cut through easily,he noted, stepping back and giving himself room.

The construct reset its stance. No aggression in the movement — just efficiency, the repositioning of something that had been designed to be difficult rather than fast. It was slightly slower than him. Not dramatically, but measurably.
He tested that margin with a straight thrust aimed at its center mass, pulling back before it could grab his blade, moving laterally before it could redirect its weight.
It tracked him accurately. Reacted without delay. But the reaction always came just after his movement rather than with it — processing, not anticipating.
It responds to what I do,he thought.It doesn’t predict.

That was useful. It meant unpredictable movement would work better than committed attacks. He was faster. If he stopped trying to cut through it and started using that speed differently, the fight changed shape.
He teleported behind it.

The construct turned — correctly, tracking the spatial displacement — but Leon was already moving laterally again before it completed the turn, and the combination of the teleport and the immediate secondary movement produced a half-second window where the construct’s tracking fell behind.
He drove his sword into the joint where its neck met its shoulder, holy energy channeled through the blade, and felt something give.

Not damage to the material. Something internal — a mechanism, a connection point, whatever translated the construct’s central function into its physical movement. The holy energy wasn’t destroying it. It was disrupting it, interfering with whatever animated the structure the way it interfered with abyssal corruption.
The construct’s left arm stopped responding.
There it is,Leon thought.

He moved faster now, the pattern clarified — targeting joints and connection points rather than trying to break the material itself, using holy energy as an interference tool rather than a destructive one. Three more strikes in quick succession: the right shoulder, the left knee, the base of its spine.
The construct went down on the fourth hit, not destroyed but fully disrupted, its animating function interrupted enough that the body simply stopped.
THUD.

Leon stood over it and caught his breath — not from exertion, just from the focused intensity of working out a problem under pressure. He’d felt fully engaged in that fight in a way that straightforward overwhelming force didn’t produce.
Good design,he thought, looking at the construct.You can’t just hit harder. You have to understand what you’re hitting.
He turned his attention back to the platform space.
The configuration had changed when he’d inserted the disc — he’d registered it happening and filed it for after the fight. Now he looked properly at what had shifted.

Roughly thirty platforms in the upper section of the space had moved, rearranging into a new pattern that hadn’t existed before. Several that had been isolated were now adjacent to each other, forming a loose chain leading toward a section of the darkness he hadn’t been able to fully map yet. At the end of that chain, further out than his spatial awareness reached comfortably, he could feel something — a density, a concentration, the sense of something significant sitting beyond his current range.
The disc had unlocked a path.
He moved along it, platform by platform, his awareness reading each one before he arrived.

The second platform on the chain held another disc — different rune configuration, different weight, corresponding to a different lock somewhere in the space. He picked it up with the same care as the first, reading its trigger layer before touching it. Slightly more complex than the previous one. He pocketed it.
The third platform held a construct identical to the one he’d just disabled, and this one engaged the moment he landed without waiting for a condition.
He dealt with it faster this time — the pattern already understood, the joint targeting already mapped. Forty seconds instead of the three minutes the first one had taken.
The fourth platform held something new.

A panel of runes carved directly into the platform’s surface, arranged in a grid pattern, each symbol capable of being pressed. There were forty-two symbols total and no instruction. Above the panel, carved into a small raised block of stone, was a single phrase in a script he didn’t recognize at first glance.
He studied it for a moment.
Upper One script,he realized slowly.The same script style from the tower’s exterior carvings.

He couldn’t read it fully. But his intelligence was high enough and his exposure to the tower’s architectural language sufficient that he could extract partial meaning from the structure of the phrase — the way certain symbol combinations repeated in patterns that suggested grammatical function rather than unique meaning.

The phrase was a question. He was almost certain of that. The structure matched interrogative formations in two other symbol systems he’d encountered. What the question was asking, he couldn’t fully determine.
He looked at the forty-two symbols in the grid.
Some of them he recognized from the disc’s rune configuration. Some matched markings he’d seen on the tower’s walls during the walk to the floor two portal. A smaller subset were entirely unfamiliar.
He didn’t press anything yet.
Instead he spent four minutes simply looking at the grid, mapping the relationships between symbols, trying to build enough of a framework to make an informed choice rather than a random one.

Patterns emerged. The familiar symbols clustered in the corners. The unfamiliar ones concentrated in the center. The symbols he recognized from the disc were distributed across the grid in a configuration that wasn’t random — they were spaced in a way that matched the disc’s own internal pattern, the same spatial relationship reproduced at larger scale.
The disc is the key and the answer,he thought.Press the symbols that match the disc’s pattern in the same relative positions.
He pressed the first symbol.
A tone sounded — low, resonant, coming from somewhere beneath the platform rather than from the panel itself.
He pressed the second. Third. Fourth. Working through the pattern he’d mapped from the disc, reproducing its spatial arrangement on the grid’s larger scale.
On the ninth press, something clicked.

The platform shuddered. The panel’s symbols went dark. And above him, in the upper darkness of the space, something massive and slow began to move — a structure he hadn’t been able to see before, lit now by a pale light that hadn’t existed a moment ago.
A door. Enormous, built into what had appeared to be empty darkness, now visible and opening.
Beyond it, the concentration he’d been feeling at the edge of his awareness resolved into something he could read clearly.
A chamber. And inside it, the sense of something waiting — not a construct, not a mechanism, something with a different quality entirely. Something that had been in there for a very long time.
Leon pocketed the second disc, checked his sword, and headed toward the door.
