A smaller subset were entirely unfamiliar.
He didn’t press anything yet.
Instead he spent four minutes simply looking at the grid, mapping the relationships between symbols, trying to build enough of a framework to make an informed choice rather than a random one.
Patterns emerged.
The familiar symbols clustered in the corners.
The unfamiliar ones concentrated in the center.

The symbols he recognized from the disc were distributed across the grid in a configuration that wasn’t random — they were spaced in a way that matched the disc’s own internal pattern, the same spatial relationship reproduced at larger scale.
The disc is the key and the answer,he thought.Press the symbols that match the disc’s pattern in the same relative positions.
He pressed the first symbol.
A tone sounded — low, resonant, coming from somewhere beneath the platform rather than from the panel itself.
He pressed the second.
Third.
Fourth.
Working through the pattern he’d mapped from the disc, reproducing its spatial arrangement on the grid’s larger scale.
On the ninth press, something clicked.
The platform shuddered.
The panel’s symbols went dark.
And above him, in the upper darkness of the space, something massive and slow began to move — a structure he hadn’t been able to see before, lit now by a pale light that hadn’t existed a moment ago.
A door.
Enormous, built into what had appeared to be empty darkness, now visible and opening.
Beyond it, the concentration he’d been feeling at the edge of his awareness resolved into something he could read clearly.
A chamber.
And inside it, the sense of something waiting — not a construct, not a mechanism, something with a different quality entirely.
Something that had been in there for a very long time.
Leon pocketed the second disc, checked his sword, and headed toward the door.

chapters.title: Chapter 540: Second Floor of the Ascension Tower—3
paragraphs: Leon entered the chamber.

It was long and narrow, the ceiling lost somewhere in darkness above, the floor flat and polished in a way the platform space hadn’t been. Torches lined the walls at regular intervals — not fire, something that produced light without heat, steady and unwavering.
And on both sides of the hall, statues.

Eight of them total, four on each side, each one different in pose and proportion but sharing one quality — they were armed. Swords, spears, a halberd on the far left, a weapon he didn’t immediately have a name for on the far right. Each one was carved with the detail of something that had been made to last rather than to impress.
At the base of each statue, carved into the stone, is a question.
Above the entrance behind him, also carved, was a single line in runic script that he could read well enough by now to extract the meaning from.
Answer correctly or do not answer at all. There is no third option.

He understood immediately. The wrong answer meant the statue moved. He stood at the entrance for a moment and took stock of all eight questions before approaching any of them, reading each base inscription from a distance with his enhanced vision.
He started at the left side, the first statue.
I speak without a mouth and hear without ears. I have no body, but I come alive with the wind. What am I?
He read it once. Echo. He’d heard this one in a different form, in a different life, and the answer arrived without effort.
He pressed his hand to the base where a small indentation waited, clearly designed for a response mechanism, and spoke the word clearly.
"Echo."
The statue didn’t move. A faint tone sounded from somewhere inside the stone — low, confirming.
He moved to the second.
The more you take, the more you leave behind. What am I?
He almost smiled. "Footsteps."
Another confirming tone.
Third statue.
I have cities, but no houses are there. I have mountains, but no trees grow there. I have water, but no fish swim there. I have roads, but no horses travel them. What am I?
He read it twice, not because he didn’t know, but because the runic translation required a moment to confirm he’d read it correctly.
"A map."
Tone. He kept moving.
Fourth statue — and here he slowed.
I am not alive, but I can grow. I have no lungs, but I need air. I have no mouth, but water kills me. What am I?
He stood in front of it for a moment, turning the three conditions over.
Not alive but grows. No lungs but needs air. No mouth but water kills it.
"Fire."
Tone.

He crossed to the right side of the hall and worked back toward the entrance. Fifth, sixth, seventh — all answerable, all producing their confirming tones. The hall felt lighter somehow after each correct answer, the atmosphere less compressed.
Then he reached the eighth statue. The last one. The one closest to the entrance, which he’d read first and set aside because something about it had felt different from the others.
He stood in front of it now and read the inscription again carefully.
What question can never be answered with yes?
He stood with it.

The obvious answer arrived immediately —are you asleep?— and he turned it over, looking for the catch. If you were asleep, you couldn’t answer. So technically correct. But the question saidnever, which was absolute, andare you asleepcould theoretically be answered yes under circumstances where someone was sleepwalking, or dreaming and speaking, or—
He set that aside and looked for something cleaner.

Are you dead?If you were dead, you couldn’t answer at all, so it could never be answered yes. But it also couldn’t be answered no by a dead person, which meant it wasn’t specifically unanswerable with yes — it was unanswerable entirely.
He spent four minutes on it. Genuine, focused engagement, running through categories of questions, testing each one against the absolute nature ofnever.

The more he worked at it, the more he felt the question resisting resolution — not because he wasn’t thinking hard enough, but because the resistance was intrinsic to the question itself. Every candidate answer he found had an edge case, an exception, a scenario where it broke down.
What if there is no answer,he thought.What if that’s the point.
The statue’s weapon arm moved.

Slowly. Deliberately. The carved stone shifted with the grinding inevitability of something that had been waiting for exactly this outcome — the question that had no answer producing the result it was always going to produce.
Leon watched the weapon rise and felt something clarify in his mind.
Why would I stand here and let it hit me?

The question had no answer. Fine. That was apparently true. But nothing in the inscription at the entrance had said he had to stand still for the consequence. It had saidto answer correctly or do not answer at all.He hadn’t answered incorrectly. He simply hadn’t answered — which was the only honest response to a question with no answer.
The statue didn’t care about that distinction.

But Leon did, and more importantly, the statue was now committed to a swing that was fully readable, fully telegraphed, the stone arm moving on a fixed arc that his spatial awareness had mapped completely before it was halfway through the motion.
He stepped inside the arc and hit it first.
Not the blade — the joint at the shoulder, holy energy driving through the connection point the way he’d learned from the constructs on the platforms. The statue’s arm locked mid-swing.
It adapted. The other arm came around.

He ducked and drove his elbow into the statue’s midsection, pure physical force rather than any technique, and felt the internal structure respond — not breaking, but compressing, something shifting inside.

The statue was faster than the platform constructs. More committed in its movements, less mechanical, closer to something that had been designed to fight rather than designed to track. It pushed back with genuine weight, and he had to work for every position, using his spatial awareness to stay ahead of a reach that was longer than his and a mass that was considerably more than his.
CRACK. CRACK. BOOM.
He took the knee joint on the third exchange, the shoulder joint on the fifth, and the base of the spine on the seventh.
The statue went down.
THUD.
He stood over it, breathing steadily, and looked at the hall around him.
All eight statues are silent. All eight questions answered — seven with words, one with something else entirely.

From the center of the chamber floor, stone ground against stone as something rose. A pillar, smooth and dark, climbing to chest height and stopping. On its surface, a handprint pressed into the material as if the stone had been soft when it was made.
Above it, carved in the same runic script as everything else in this tower, was a phrase he read carefully and translated as best he could.
Those who forget may enter. Those who remember may survive.
A notification appeared before he’d finished processing what that meant.
[Memory suppression: initiating.]
He looked at the handprint.

The pull toward it was immediate and specific — not compulsion exactly, more the quality of a door that was clearly meant to be opened and was waiting for the person who’d earned the right to open it.
He placed his hand against the stone.
The chamber disappeared.

chapters.title: Chapter 541: Second Floor of the Ascension Tower—4
paragraphs: Leon opened his eyes.

Dirt floor. The smell of wood smoke and something cooking — root vegetables and whatever the season allowed. Morning light came through a single window cut directly into the wall, no glass, just an opening with a cloth hung over it that moved in the breeze.
He sat up from a straw mattress and looked at his hands.

Small. The hands of a child, eight years old at most, the knuckles unformed, the palms soft. He turned them over and back, and felt nothing unusual about doing so, because he was Kaen, and he had always been Kaen, and these were simply his hands.
His mother called from the other room.
He got up, ate breakfast, and went outside for chores.

The village was forty people on the edge of a forest that nobody entered after dark. That was simply a fact of life, like hard winters and short summers. You didn’t discuss it because discussing it made the days harder to get through.
Kaen was quiet and methodical in a way that the adults around him occasionally noticed without being able to articulate why. He didn’t think much about it. He was just good at things.
The night the creatures came, he was eight years and four months old.
He heard them before he saw them.
Something in the quality of the forest’s nighttime silence changed — a wrongness his body registered before his mind did — and he was sitting up in the dark before the first scream reached the house.
His father’s voice, low and urgent:get your sister, get under the floor.

He grabbed Ren’s arm. She woke confused and started to make a sound, and he put his hand over her mouth — firm, communicatingnot nowrather thanbe afraid— and pulled her toward the corner where the loose floorboard was.
They went under. The board went back above them. Ren shook against him in the dark, and he held her and counted his own breathing until it steadied.
The sounds outside were bad. He didn’t fully process what they meant.
When the floorboard tore away from above, the creature looking down into the gap found them immediately. Large. Wrong in its proportions, limbs too long, head too flat. It reached down.
Something happened in Kaen’s right hand.

Not a thought. His hand came up, and his fingers arranged themselves in a configuration he had never consciously learned, and from that arrangement something extended outward — invisible, weightless, present in a way he had no language for. He didn’t know what it was. He didn’t know that in another life he would have called it spatial energy, would have recognized it as an extension of an affinity he’d spent months developing, would have understood exactly what he’d just done and why it worked.
Here, he only knew that his hand had done something, and the creature had stopped.
Frozen in place above the gap, its reach interrupted, its forward motion simply absent.
One second. Two.
His father came from the side.
After the village counted its losses and morning came gray and quiet, Kaen sat on the step outside and looked at his right hand.

There was something in it. Not a feeling exactly — more like a pressure, a potential, the sense of a word he knew the shape of but couldn’t pronounce yet. Something that had been there his whole life, he thought, in the way that things could be present without being noticed until they were needed.
He pressed his fingers together the way they’d arranged themselves in the dark.
Nothing happened.
He tried again, differently, and felt the faintest response — a resistance in the air just in front of his palm, barely there, gone before he could examine it.
His father came and sat beside him. Neither of them spoke about it. Eventually, his mother called them inside.
Years passed.

The thing in his hand — he had no better name for it, onlythe thing in his hand— developed not through training but through use. When danger was present, it surfaced with a clarity and ease that startled him. When danger was absent, it receded into that background pressure, available but quiet.

By twelve, he’d understood it affected space in some way. Objects moved when he didn’t touch them. Distance behaved differently when he focused. He couldn’t have explained the mechanism because he had no framework for it — in this world, in Kaen’s world, there was no vocabulary for what he was doing. People who could do unusual things existed, but what they did had names and traditions and teachers.
What Kaen did had none of those things. It was simply his, appearing from nowhere, answering to instinct rather than instruction.
The other thing appeared later.

He was fourteen, badly injured in a farming accident — a cut deep enough that his father’s face had gone pale looking at it — and something warm moved through his hand as he pressed it against the wound. Not the spatial thing. Different. Softer, if energy could be soft. It moved through the injury, and the bleeding slowed faster than it should have, the tissue responding in ways that his father watched with an expression he couldn’t quite categorize.

He didn’t know the word holy. He didn’t know the word energy in the sense he would have used it in another life. He only knew that his hand could do two different things, and that the second one was warm where the first one was precise, and that together they made him something that didn’t fit the available categories in any world he’d found himself in.

He kept both of them quiet. Not from shame — from the practical understanding that things people couldn’t categorize made them uncomfortable, and uncomfortable people made poor company and sometimes worse enemies.
By seventeen, the creatures from the forest had pushed into the valleys beyond his village, and the region was organizing.
He enlisted.

The army was the first time he’d been around enough people to see clearly what different looked like from the outside. The other recruits were capable — some genuinely, fighters with real training and tactical education.
They were not like Kaen.

He didn’t announce it. He simply did what was asked and occasionally did more when the situation required, and the results spoke plainly enough that conclusions formed around him without his participation.

In a river valley engagement where everything went wrong simultaneously, he held a position that shouldn’t have been holdable, using the spatial thing in ways that the people beside him saw as instinct or luck or talent rather than what it actually was. Nobody died in his section who didn’t have to die.
They gave him a name after that. The old convention — earned rather than assigned.
Varek.The one that the storm moves around.
He didn’t argue.

The women came with the reputation. Some of them were extraordinary — genuinely, in their own right. A healer attached to the third division was someone whose thinking he respected and whose company he returned to when campaigns allowed.
But he didn’t fall for any of it.

Not from indifference. From something underneath Kaen, underneath Varek, underneath nine years of built life — a quality he recognized without being able to source. A warmth he already had, somewhere he couldn’t access from here, that made every other warmth feel like a reflection of the real thing rather than the thing itself.
He knew he belonged somewhere else.
The healer asked him once why he always seemed like he was waiting.
He thought about it honestly.
"I think I already have what I’m looking for," he said. "I just can’t remember where I left it."
She looked at him for a long moment. "That’s either the most romantic or the most tragic thing I’ve ever heard."
He smiled and didn’t try to explain.

The fragments came faster as years accumulated — a reflex in a fight that no one had taught Kaen, a spatial read that went beyond anything this world’s experience had given him, a relationship with certain energies that felt remembered rather than learned.
He didn’t examine them too directly. They worked when he needed them.

By twenty-three, he was leading significant engagements. By twenty-six, with the creatures pushing into every major city’s territory, he was one of four commanders coordinating the response across the region.
He was good at this.
Different in kind,said the general who had watched him since his first enlistment.Not just a degree.
Somewhere underneath Kaen, underneath Varek, underneath all of it — something heard that and almost surfaced.
Almost.

chapters.title: Chapter 542: Second Floor of the Ascension Tower—5
paragraphs: The creatures didn’t come from one direction.

That was the first thing Varek understood when the reports started arriving — not a front, not a push from the forest’s edge outward, but emergence from multiple points simultaneously, as though the forest itself had decided to produce them rather than harbor them. Villages in three valleys were hit on the same night. Four settlements have gone dark within a week. The pattern wasn’t expansion. It was coordination.
He stood over the map with the other three commanders and said what the map was showing.
"It’s not a migration," he said. "Something is directing them."
The oldest of the four, a woman named Sera who had been fighting these creatures longer than Varek had been alive, looked at the map for a long time without speaking.
"We’ve suspected that for two years," she said finally. "We didn’t say it out loud because saying it out loud meant we had to find the source."

Varek looked at the distribution of attacks. The pattern had a center — not obvious, not geometric, but present in the way that the absence of attacks in one particular region was too consistent to be a coincidence. Everything was pushing outward from a point roughly sixty kilometers into the deepest section of the forest.
"Then we find the source," he said.
The campaign took eight months.

Not because the distance was great, but because the forest was not a passive obstacle. The creatures operated differently inside it than they did in settled land — more coordinated, responding faster, as though the trees themselves were carrying information about where the forces were and what they were doing.

Varek lost people. Not carelessly — he was meticulous about casualties in a way that made some of the older officers uncomfortable, because most commanders at his level had accepted a certain accounting of acceptable loss that he refused to accept. He knew the name of every death. Every name he carried forward.
But he lost people, because that was the reality of moving sixty kilometers into a forest that was actively trying to prevent it.

The spatial thing in his right hand developed enormously during those eight months. Not from training — from necessity, from encountering situations that demanded more than he currently had and adapting to produce it. He could feel the distances between things in a way that went beyond sight. Could manipulate the position of objects and people in space with a precision and range that grew month by month. Could move himself through space in ways that the soldiers around him had stopped questioning because they’d seen the results too many times to waste energy on the impossibility.
He still had no name for it. He’d stopped needing one.

The warm thing — the other ability, the one that moved differently, that felt like it came from somewhere different from the spatial one — was what kept his people alive when the spatial one couldn’t reach. Injuries that should have been fatal slowed. Soldiers who should have died in the night were standing in the morning. He was quiet about it, moved through the camp after dark, and nobody discussed it because discussing it would have required finding words for something that didn’t have words.
He was Varek. The storm moved around him. Things were different when he was present.
That was the available vocabulary, and everyone used it.
The source was a structure.

Not natural — built, ancient, the construction predating anything in the regional historical record. Stone that had weathered to the color of old bone, covered in markings he didn’t recognize, set into a clearing at the forest’s center where the trees grew around it rather than through it, leaving a perfect circle of open ground.

The creatures were densest here. Not massed in the way an army massed — layered, distributed, with a depth and complexity that suggested the structure was the point they were protecting rather than the point they were using.
He spent three days at the perimeter with Sera and the remaining commanders, watching the patterns of movement, mapping the coverage, finding the gaps.
On the fourth day, he went in.

Not alone — he wasn’t careless about his own life any more than he was careless about his people’s — but with a small group, fast and quiet, chosen for endurance rather than raw combat capability because endurance was what the approach required.
The fight to reach the structure took six hours and cost him two of the seven people he’d brought. He carried both names forward.
Inside the structure, the creatures stopped coming.
That was the first strange thing. The moment he crossed the threshold, the pursuit simply ended, the creatures outside maintaining their positions but not following.

The interior was a single large chamber, the stone walls lined with the same markings as the exterior. In the center, elevated on a plinth, something pulsed with a light that wasn’t quite light — more the impression of light, the suggestion of illumination without the heat or the directionality.

He felt both of his abilities respond to it immediately. The spatial thing in his right hand recognized something in the pulse — a resonance, a correspondence, as though whatever was producing that light was operating on a related principle. The warm thing in him pushed back against it, not defensively but in the way two forces push against each other when they occupy the same space.
He approached.

The pulse intensified with each step. Not threateningly — it was reading him; he understood that, the way his spatial awareness read environments. Something in the structure was assessing what had walked in.
He placed his hand on the plinth.
The creatures outside went silent simultaneously.
Then the light expanded, and the chamber was full of it, and the fragments that had been surfacing for nine years stopped being fragments.
His name was Leon.

Not Kaen. Not Varek. Leon. The name landed in him like a key finding a lock, and everything else came with it — world, history, people, the specific warmth he’d been carrying without source for nine years suddenly having a face and a name and a place.
Seraphine. Ira. Vyra. Loriel.
The tower. The second floor. The pillar, the handprint, and the phrase about forgetting and remembering.
He stood in the ancient chamber with his hand on the plinth and was fully, completely himself for the first time in nine years.
The light around him shifted.

A tone sounded — not from the chamber, from somewhere deeper, from the trial itself — and the assessment recalibrated in real time around what he actually was rather than what it had been testing for.

The creatures outside didn’t just go silent. They dissolved. Every one of them, simultaneously, the light from the chamber expanding outward through the forest in a wave that consumed them as it moved, the coordination that had been directing them was interrupted at the source.
The structure shook. The plinth went dark.

The instance held for one more moment — the forest outside, Sera and the others waiting at the perimeter, the weight of nine years of a life lived completely, the names of the people he’d lost and the names of the people he hadn’t — and then it released.

The instance held for one final moment — the forest outside, Sera and the others waiting at the perimeter, nine years of a life lived completely, the names of people lost and people saved — and then released.
[INSTANCE COMPLETE]
[Duration: 9 years, 2 months, 14 days — Compressed]
[Performance Evaluation: EX]
[Memory Suppression Resistance: Anomaly Title Override Detected — Full Identity Retention Across Entire Duration]
[Adaptive Difficulty: Final Recalibration Applied at Memory Restoration Point]
[Combat Efficiency: EX]
[Leadership Assessment: EX]
[Suppression Resistance: EX — First recorded instance of complete identity retention under Tower Grade suppression]
[Overall Grade: EX — First ever recorded on Floor Two]
[Rewards Calculating...]

chapters.title: Chapter 543: Second Floor of the Ascension Tower—6
paragraphs: [Overall Grade: EX — First ever recorded on Floor Two]
[Rewards Calculating...]
A pause. Longer than any notification pause he’d experienced before, as though whatever system ran beneath the tower was doing something more involved than pulling from a predetermined list.
Then:
[PRIMARY REWARD]
Void Dominion — Spatial Mastery: Transcendent

Your relationship with space has fundamentally changed. You no longer move through space. You fold it. Objects, attacks, people, terrain — the space around them bends to your will. Compression, expansion, redirection — all are available as direct extensions of intent. Range ceiling: removed. This is not an upgrade to teleportation. Teleportation exists within this.
Leon read that twice.
Fold it,he thought. Do not move through it. Fold it.

He flexed his right hand slowly, feeling the difference immediately — the spatial awareness that had always extended outward from him now felt different in quality, like the difference between looking at something and being able to reach into it. The space around his hand responded to the flex in a way it hadn’t before, the air compressing slightly at his fingertips, reality briefly agreeing to be a different shape before returning.
He kept reading.
[SECONDARY REWARD]
Echo of Varek — Nine-Year Combat Integration

The life lived within the instance does not end with the instance. Nine years of battlefield experience, tactical leadership, and combat refinement are permanently embedded below conscious thought. This is not memory-requiring access. This is a reflex. Your body knows things before your mind decides them. Integration: complete.

He noticed this one immediately too — not as a feeling but as an absence of the slight delay that had always existed between perceiving a threat and responding to it. Something had closed that gap. He didn’t have to think to know what to do. The thinking happened underneath, faster than thinking.
[TERTIARY REWARD]
Title Acquired: Suppression Breaker (Mythic)

You resisted Tower Grade memory suppression through identity alone across nine years of compressed instance time. No external tool, no system assist, no prepared countermeasure. You simply remembered who you were against a force designed to make you forget. Permanent immunity to all identity alteration, memory suppression, and forced persona effects below Divine Grade. The tower acknowledges you broke something it believed unbreakable.
A new title. Mythic grade. He added it to the list without ceremony and kept going.
[FOURTH REWARD]
Legendary Instance Seed — One

A self-contained instance, different in nature from the one you experienced. Repeatable. Scalable to whoever enters — the difficulty and reward calibrate to the entrant’s level and capability. Plant it within a bound world under your authority, and it takes root permanently. Those who complete it earn real rewards. Those who attempt it and fail leave empty-handed. It cannot be replicated. It cannot be transferred. There is only one.
It came from the tower. Now it is yours.

A small crystalline object materialized in his palm — roughly the size of a closed fist, faceted, pulsing with a slow internal light that moved like something breathing. It was warm. Not the warmth of temperature — the warmth of something alive in the way that very old, very significant things were alive.
He closed his fingers around it carefully.
Plant it in the dimensional world,he thought.And it becomes a resource. A permanent one. People can enter, earn real rewards, and grow from it.

He thought about the Pyrans. About the humans. About fifteen thousand people in his world were training on cores and ambient mana and whatever the world fragment merger had produced, and who would now have access to a repeatable instance that scaled to them and paid out real rewards on completion.
The fourth reward was quietly the most significant thing on the list in terms of long-term impact, and it had been listed fourth.
He was still thinking about it when the final notification appeared.
[HIDDEN REWARD]

A single line of runic script materialized in the air in front of him — not part of the standard notification format, not bracketed or labeled, just present, as though the tower itself had decided to say something outside its own system.
It held for three seconds.
[Ascension Tower Second Floor Acknowledgment Received]
You were not supposed to remember. You were not supposed to survive remembering. The tower does not give this floor to many. It has never given this rating to anyone.
Then it was gone. Completely. No record of it in his notification history, no system log, nothing. As though it had been said rather than displayed.
[FLOOR TWO: CLEARED]
[Portal to Floor Three: Now accessible]
Leon stood in the chamber for a long moment after the notifications cleared.

The obsidian pillar was dark beside him, its handprint smooth and unremarkable now, nothing in it suggesting what it had produced. The hall behind him was silent. Eight statues, seven answered and one fought through, all motionless.
He looked at the crystalline seed in his closed hand, opened his fingers, and studied it in the steady torchlight.

Nine years. Compressed, yes — but lived fully, every day of them real within the instance’s logic. Kaen, who became Varek, saved a world that didn’t exist. People he’d lost whose names he still carried. A healer who’d asked him why he always seemed like he was waiting and hadn’t gotten a complete answer.
The weight of it was real, even though the world wasn’t.
He pocketed the seed carefully in the inventory connected to his soul.

Then he checked his sword, rolled his right hand once more — feeling the Void Dominion sitting in it like something that had always been there and had simply decided to reveal its full nature — and turned toward the Portal beside the floor three.
The one leading to the Tower main hall, which led to the exit, he didn’t know how much time in reality had passed; he was a bit anxious and hoped not too much time had passed.

Hoping he hadn’t missed the Seraphine and other Class Reawakening Dungeon Trials, right now, he felt relieved that he had left them in the care of Xyra, or else he would have worried out of his mind for them.

chapters.title: Chapter 544: Preparations Before the Awakening Dungeon
paragraphs: Leon stepped through the portal and was back in the tower’s main hall.

The grand lounge opened around him exactly as he’d left it — the same steady, unwavering light, the same circular reception desk at the center, the same architectural weight of something built to outlast everything around it.
Behind the desk, the elf looked up immediately.

Her golden eyes found him before he’d taken a full step into the space, the attention in them sharpening with the focused quality of someone who had been waiting and was now watching to see if this time would be different from last time.
Leon didn’t break stride.

He found the exit and walked toward it with the same uninterrupted pace he’d used on the way in, the crystalline seed warm in his pocket, the Void Dominion sitting in his right hand like something that had always been there and had finally decided to show its full shape.
The elf watched him cross the entire hall without slowing.
Her expression didn’t change while he was looking in her direction. The moment he passed through the exit and the tower door closed behind him, she let out a breath through her teeth.
"Ridiculous," she said, to no one in particular.
Then she hmph’d and looked back at the desk in front of her.
Outside, the dimensional world’s ambient light settled over him — familiar, soft, the sourceless glow that had become as natural to him as actual sunlight.
He turned and looked at the tower behind him.

Then, almost involuntarily, his gaze moved to the structure just visible beyond it — Xyra’s mansion, the red-themed complex she’d built on the other side without mentioning it, its presence detectable now that he knew to look for it.
He entertained the thought of going there for exactly one second.
Then he extended his spatial awareness outward through the world’s connection, found what he was looking for, and teleported.

The mountain plateau materialized around him — the familiar training ground, the house sitting solid to one side, the open rocky space where he and Seraphine had spent months working through techniques and skills and each other.

Seraphine was in motion when he arrived, working through a sequence with her katana that he recognized as a refinement of something she’d been developing before he left. She felt him the moment he appeared — he saw it in the slight change of her movement, the sequence completing itself before she turned.
She crossed the distance between them fast and jumped.
He caught her.

Her arms went around his neck and her legs wrapped around him and she kissed him before either of them said a word — deep and immediate and completely unambiguous, the kind of kiss that had nine days of missing in it compressed into a single point of contact. He felt her tongue against his and responded in kind, and held her with both arms while the world was briefly just this.
When it ended, there was a moment where they were still close enough that a thread of connection pulled between them before finally breaking.
He looked at her face. She was already looking at his lips again.
"How long?" he asked.
She took a moment to redirect her attention. "Nine days."
He exhaled slowly.

Nine years inside. Nine days outside. The ratio had held almost exactly, the instance’s compression matching the dimensional world’s dilation in a way that shouldn’t have been surprising given the tower’s evident sophistication but that still landed with relief.
Ten to fifteen days before the class reawakening dungeon opened. Xyra had said that before he’d entered the tower. The bare minimum hadn’t even been reached yet.
There’s still time,he thought.Enough of it if we move properly.

Seraphine hadn’t loosened her grip. Her legs were still around him, her arms still at his neck, and she was looking at his mouth with an expression that communicated clearly that one kiss had not resolved whatever the nine days had built up.

He thought about the cradle of elemental seed sitting in the cosmic shop — eight hundred million causality, the item he’d been watching for months, the one that would push his foundation to a qualitatively different level before the dungeon opened. He’d had nine hundred million during the battle, and that was before the final phase of the fight had finished.
He was going to be extraordinarily wealthy in causality right now.

He gave her another kiss — long, unhurried, genuinely meant — and then set her down and spent the next twenty minutes walking through what she needed to focus on before the dungeon. Her light affinity, her lightning affinity, the foundational understanding of both that would let her reconstruct skills and techniques from scratch inside an environment that stripped everything back to level one.

Xyra had explained it clearly: the dungeon removed status, levels, and the system scaffolding on which skills and techniques were built. But it couldn’t remove understanding. If the foundation was deep enough, if the comprehension was real rather than system-granted, those things could be rebuilt from the inside through will and knowledge alone.
That was what mattered. Not the skill stones, not the technique scrolls. The actual understanding underneath them.

Seraphine listened with the focused attention of someone who had been thinking about this for nine days already and was now receiving confirmation of what she’d suspected. When he finished, she nodded once, turned back to her training, and was already moving before he’d stepped away.
He teleported to Ira’s mountain.

She saw him materialize and was already moving toward him with the specific momentum of someone who had decided on a course of action and was executing it without intermediate steps. Her hands went to the front of his clothes before he’d fully registered her intention.
"Ira."
She stopped. Blinked. Pulled her hands back.
"I was joking," she said, and stuck her tongue out.

He looked at her for a moment. She met his eyes with the completely guileless expression of someone who had absolutely not been joking and was relying on the assertion to carry more weight than the evidence supported.
"Sure," he said.
She grinned.

He gave her the same instruction he’d given Seraphine — foundation over everything, affinity comprehension, techniques understood deeply enough to rebuild from nothing. He punctuated it with two kisses that she received with considerable enthusiasm and zero subtlety, and then he teleported to Loriel’s mountain before the situation developed further.

Loriel was practicing with her cane when he arrived, working through healing formations in the air in front of her, the life element moving in patterns he could read as genuine technical development rather than repetition. She’d been working seriously.
She looked at him and waited.

He didn’t immediately move toward her, and she noticed the absence of what she might have expected — the greeting, the contact. She held his gaze for a moment and then, with the specific courage of someone making a small decision they’ve been deliberating over, said: "You won’t even give me a hug."
Not quite a question. Not quite a statement.
He crossed the space and gave her one.

She held on for a beat longer than necessary, and he let her. They weren’t anything officially — no declaration, no established arrangement, just the complicated honest reality of two people who occupied a particular kind of closeness without having named it. He gave her the same instruction as the others, focusing specifically on her life element foundation and her technique comprehension.
She listened carefully.

When he was about to teleport, she kissed his cheek with the speed of someone who had calculated they had a one-second window and was using every millisecond of it; of course, if he had wanted, he would have easily dodged her sneak attack.
He arrived on Vyra’s mountain.
And stopped.
The air was different here. Warmer — not temperature exactly, but quality, the ambient energy on this mountain carrying heat that the others hadn’t had. He understood why immediately.
Vyra sat cross-legged on the rock twenty meters ahead of him, and around her, the fire was alive.

Not burning — alive was the accurate word. It moved with intention rather than physics, curling in patterns that responded to something internal to her rather than to wind or fuel, the flames circling her in slow, deliberate rotations that had the quality of something being directed rather than something simply burning.
He recognized what he was looking at.

Level five Aura. She was taking the step from four to five. The transition he hadn’t managed himself in any of his affinities yet — the qualitative shift that turned an affinity into something that operated at a categorically different level.
He stopped where he was and didn’t move closer.
The flames near the perimeter of her circle pulsed once in his direction — a single, sharp outward breath of heat — and settled back. Not aggressive. Just aware.
Don’t interrupt,the fire said, in the language that fire used.
He understood.
He created a chair from ice, placed it on the rock a safe distance back, and sat down.

This was learning. He didn’t know exactly what the step from level four to level five felt like from inside — he had theories, he had the intellectual framework, but watching someone who’d lived for centuries make the transition in real time was information he couldn’t get any other way.
He watched.
And simultaneously, with the multi-tasking capability that fifteen thousand intelligences produced almost as a side effect, he opened the cosmic shop.
The translucent golden screen materialized in front of him, hovering in the air between him and the training scene, perfectly readable while his eyes stayed primarily on Vyra.
He went directly to what he needed.

The Cradle of Elemental Seed sat where it always had in the shop’s inventory — eight hundred million causality, the item he’d been watching since he first saw it, the one that would change his elemental foundation at a level that none of the individual skill stones or technique scrolls could reach.
He checked his current causality balance.
The number that appeared made him go very still for exactly one second.

sentences.text: Leon stepped through the portal and was back in the tower’s main hall.

The grand lounge opened around him exactly as he’d left it — the same steady, unwavering light, the same circular reception desk at the center, the same architectural weight of something built to outlast everything around it.
Behind the desk, the elf looked up immediately.

Her golden eyes found him before he’d taken a full step into the space, the attention in them sharpening with the focused quality of someone who had been waiting and was now watching to see if this time would be different from last time.
Leon didn’t break stride.

He found the exit and walked toward it with the same uninterrupted pace he’d used on the way in, the crystalline seed warm in his pocket, the Void Dominion sitting in his right hand like something that had always been there and had finally decided to show its full shape.
The elf watched him cross the entire hall without slowing.
Her expression didn’t change while he was looking in her direction.
The moment he passed through the exit and the tower door closed behind him, she let out a breath through her teeth.
"Ridiculous," she said, to no one in particular.
Then she hmph’d and looked back at the desk in front of her.
Outside, the dimensional world’s ambient light settled over him — familiar, soft, the sourceless glow that had become as natural to him as actual sunlight.
He turned and looked at the tower behind him.

Then, almost involuntarily, his gaze moved to the structure just visible beyond it — Xyra’s mansion, the red-themed complex she’d built on the other side without mentioning it, its presence detectable now that he knew to look for it.
He entertained the thought of going there for exactly one second.
Then he extended his spatial awareness outward through the world’s connection, found what he was looking for, and teleported.

The mountain plateau materialized around him — the familiar training ground, the house sitting solid to one side, the open rocky space where he and Seraphine had spent months working through techniques and skills and each other.
Seraphine was in motion when he arrived, working through a sequence with her katana that he recognized as a refinement of something she’d been developing before he left.
She felt him the moment he appeared — he saw it in the slight change of her movement, the sequence completing itself before she turned.
She crossed the distance between them fast and jumped.
He caught her.

Her arms went around his neck and her legs wrapped around him and she kissed him before either of them said a word — deep and immediate and completely unambiguous, the kind of kiss that had nine days of missing in it compressed into a single point of contact.
He felt her tongue against his and responded in kind, and held her with both arms while the world was briefly just this.
When it ended, there was a moment where they were still close enough that a thread of connection pulled between them before finally breaking.
He looked at her face.
She was already looking at his lips again.
"How long?" he asked.
She took a moment to redirect her attention.
"Nine days."
He exhaled slowly.
Nine years inside.
Nine days outside.

The ratio had held almost exactly, the instance’s compression matching the dimensional world’s dilation in a way that shouldn’t have been surprising given the tower’s evident sophistication but that still landed with relief.
Ten to fifteen days before the class reawakening dungeon opened.
Xyra had said that before he’d entered the tower.
The bare minimum hadn’t even been reached yet.
There’s still time,he thought.Enough of it if we move properly.
Seraphine hadn’t loosened her grip.

Her legs were still around him, her arms still at his neck, and she was looking at his mouth with an expression that communicated clearly that one kiss had not resolved whatever the nine days had built up.

He thought about the cradle of elemental seed sitting in the cosmic shop — eight hundred million causality, the item he’d been watching for months, the one that would push his foundation to a qualitatively different level before the dungeon opened.
He’d had nine hundred million during the battle, and that was before the final phase of the fight had finished.
He was going to be extraordinarily wealthy in causality right now.
He gave her another kiss — long, unhurried, genuinely meant — and then set her down and spent the next twenty minutes walking through what she needed to focus on before the dungeon.

Her light affinity, her lightning affinity, the foundational understanding of both that would let her reconstruct skills and techniques from scratch inside an environment that stripped everything back to level one.
Xyra had explained it clearly: the dungeon removed status, levels, and the system scaffolding on which skills and techniques were built.
But it couldn’t remove understanding.
If the foundation was deep enough, if the comprehension was real rather than system-granted, those things could be rebuilt from the inside through will and knowledge alone.
That was what mattered.
Not the skill stones, not the technique scrolls.
The actual understanding underneath them.
Seraphine listened with the focused attention of someone who had been thinking about this for nine days already and was now receiving confirmation of what she’d suspected.
When he finished, she nodded once, turned back to her training, and was already moving before he’d stepped away.
He teleported to Ira’s mountain.
She saw him materialize and was already moving toward him with the specific momentum of someone who had decided on a course of action and was executing it without intermediate steps.
Her hands went to the front of his clothes before he’d fully registered her intention.
"Ira."
She stopped.
Blinked.
Pulled her hands back.
"I was joking," she said, and stuck her tongue out.
He looked at her for a moment.
She met his eyes with the completely guileless expression of someone who had absolutely not been joking and was relying on the assertion to carry more weight than the evidence supported.
"Sure," he said.
She grinned.
He gave her the same instruction he’d given Seraphine — foundation over everything, affinity comprehension, techniques understood deeply enough to rebuild from nothing.
He punctuated it with two kisses that she received with considerable enthusiasm and zero subtlety, and then he teleported to Loriel’s mountain before the situation developed further.

Loriel was practicing with her cane when he arrived, working through healing formations in the air in front of her, the life element moving in patterns he could read as genuine technical development rather than repetition.
She’d been working seriously.
She looked at him and waited.
He didn’t immediately move toward her, and she noticed the absence of what she might have expected — the greeting, the contact.
She held his gaze for a moment and then, with the specific courage of someone making a small decision they’ve been deliberating over, said: "You won’t even give me a hug."
Not quite a question.
Not quite a statement.
He crossed the space and gave her one.
She held on for a beat longer than necessary, and he let her.
They weren’t anything officially — no declaration, no established arrangement, just the complicated honest reality of two people who occupied a particular kind of closeness without having named it.

She listened carefully.

chapters.title: Chapter 545: Preparations Before the Awakening Dungeon—1
paragraphs: Leon checked his causality balance.
[Current Causality: 1,512,340,000]
He stared at it for a full second.
One point five billion.

He’d run rough estimates during the battle — tracking kill counts, calculating rough multipliers for the Archon-ranked beasts, the Sage-ranked cannon fodder — and the math had suggested something significant. Seeing it in actual digits was still different from expecting it.
One hundred million or so had been sitting there from before the fight. The rest had come from the horde outside the City of Light in the space of a few long hours.
He let the number settle, felt the genuine, uncomplicated thrill of it, and opened the shop properly.

Vyra sat twenty meters ahead of him, still cross-legged, the fire around her moving in patterns that had nothing to do with wind. He kept her in his peripheral vision while the translucent golden screen hovered between them. His intelligence handled both without difficulty — the training observation and the shopping running in parallel, neither suffering for it.
He went to the equipment first.
Seraphine.

He thought about her as he browsed — the specific quality of how she moved, the way her combat style was built around being completely unimpeded. Lightning and light working together, precise and fast. She didn’t need armor that absorbed hits. She needed armor that didn’t exist as a constraint.
He found it quickly.
Stormveil Regalia (Epic – Armor Set)
Ultralight composite weave. Increases lightning affinity response by 40%. Reduces air resistance to movement by 60%. No encumbrance penalty.
Vendor: Silverwind Tailor
She’ll move in that like she’s wearing nothing, he thought, and bought it.

The weapon took longer because he cared about the details. She’d kept the katana he gave her past the point where most people upgraded — had built something with that design, a relationship with the shape and weight of it. He wasn’t breaking that.
He searched specifically. Katana type. Lightning and light compatible. Epic ranked.
Radiant Edge — Thunderveil Katana (Epic – Weapon)
Blade forged from condensed lightning-steel threaded with light-element crystal veins. Conducts both affinities simultaneously without interference. Increases dual-element output by 35% on strike.
Vendor: Stormforge Hana

He read the design description and felt immediate certainty. The shape was right. The balance notes matched how she held a blade. She was going to love it and wouldn’t admit how much for at least a day.
He bought it.
Ira.

Different calculation. Where Seraphine was precise, Ira was committed — full power, forward momentum, the kind of fighter who didn’t redirect so much as overwhelm. Her fire ran genuinely hot, hotter than most fire users he’d encountered, and she’d push it further in the dungeon.
The armor needed to handle heat from inside as much as from outside.
Ember Sovereign Set (Epic – Armor Set)
Forged from volcanic ironweave. Immune to heat damage from the wearer’s own affinity output. Enhances fire affinity intensity by 45%. Increases physical impact resistance by 30%.
Vendor: Cinderkeep Forge
She can go as hot as she wants and it won’t burn through her own equipment, he thought. Bought it.
Her weapon was simpler — she’d always used a spear, with the natural ease of someone for whom it was simply the correct extension of how she thought about combat.
Blazing Fang Spear (Epic – Weapon)

Spear shaft and head forged as a single piece from fire-tempered dragonsteel. Fire affinity compatibility: native — grows with the wielder’s affinity rather than capping at the current level. Increases fire output on thrust by 50%.
Vendor: Ashblood Weaponsmith
Grows with her, he noted. She’ll push that listing past its current display over.
He bought it and felt good about the choice.
Vyra.

He paused here longer than the others. She’d been leading people in combat since before his concept of a long time had any meaning. The wrong choice would be more obvious to her than to anyone else. He didn’t want to give her something she’d tolerate. He wanted something she’d respect.
He thought about how she moved. Economical. Nothing wasted. She committed to a strike only after she’d already decided it was landing.
Crimson Sovereign Plating (Epic – Armor Set)

Segmented design — each piece is independent, with zero movement restriction. Fire affinity enhancement passive: ambient heat is absorbed and converted to affinity output. Increases fire Aura intensity by 40%.
Vendor: Pyrewing Armorer
It feeds from the environment, he thought. She’ll appreciate that. Nothing wasted, including what’s already in the air around her.

The spear took the most time. She’d been using weapons longer than most civilizations had existed — she had opinions, and those opinions were probably correct. He looked for something that would feel like a choice rather than an assignment.
Sovereign’s Lance — Eternal Flame (Epic – Weapon)

Ancient alloy construction. Fire affinity resonance: deep-structural rather than surface-enchanted. The weapon responds to the wielder’s intent rather than technique — output scales with the user’s understanding of fire rather than rank. No ceiling.
Vendor: Ageless Forge — Keeper Unknown
Scales with understanding, not rank. He read that twice. For someone who’s been developing that understanding for centuries, there’s genuinely no ceiling.
He bought it.
Loriel.

One item. He’d thought about this carefully. The situation between them wasn’t officially named, and buying her the same volume as his confirmed partners would generate questions he didn’t want to navigate while dungeon preparations were underway. Seraphine noticed everything.

One well-chosen defensive artifact was defensible. She was a healer going into a dungeon where healers died first because they were the priority target for anything intelligent enough to understand what they were.
Sanctuary Veil (Epic – Artifact, Passive)

Generates a reactive barrier that activates the moment the wearer takes damage, absorbing the first strike fully regardless of source. Cooldown: 60 seconds. Cannot be destroyed by indirect or area effects.
Vendor: Warden’s Guild — Anonymous
First strike absorbed, no matter what hits her. She wouldn’t see what was coming in that dungeon. This gave her one moment to respond instead of none.
He bought it.
Revival treasures next.

Seraphine and Ira both had one each from before. He bought two more for each — three total, the threshold he’d decided between prepared and excessive. The phoenix-feature revival treasure he usually bought at the lower price tier had two units left. He took both immediately. Then five standard ones are distributed across all four of them.

Ira’s father got one. Standard tier, not a Phoenix feather. Leon thought about it for exactly one moment — the history between them, the complicated reality of that relationship — and bought it anyway. Ira would be devastated if something happened to him. That was sufficient reason.

He moved through mana recovery artifacts, healing pieces for the general dungeon population, potions in bulk — two thousand one hundred mana potions, two thousand one hundred healing potions, each costing ten thousand causality. The numbers were large, and the spending was fast, and he didn’t slow down for either.

For the broader dungeon group — nine hundred and seventy people confirmed, he’d learned from his clone’s exchange with Xyra — he bought one thousand rare-ranked healing artifacts and one thousand rare-ranked mana recovery artifacts. At the quality tier he was targeting, each normally ranged from one hundred thousand to two hundred and fifty thousand casualties. Buying two thousand of them at once gave him enough leverage to secure a bulk price averaging around one hundred and eighty thousand causality per artifact.

All of it lent. Not given. People who came back with satisfactory results received them permanently. People who didn’t return them. He was providing more support than anyone entering a class-reawakening dungeon had a right to expect — that was his choice, and he made it without reservation. But he wasn’t running a charity, and there was a difference between generosity and simply handing valuable resources away without expectation.

For weapons and armor for the general group, he had over a hundred rare-ranked pieces already in inventory. Whatever gap remained, Luna would help fill. Asking her wasn’t shameless — that was simply what it meant to have people who trusted you.
Additional items for Seraphine and Ira specifically — a ring each with resistance to illusion and mind-control effects, a spatial anchor pendant for Seraphine, a concealment artifact for Ira.
For Vyra — nothing additional. Her strength put her above the threshold where anything he was buying today would meaningfully contribute. He trusted her capability more than he trusted the items.
He checked the balance when he finished.
The number was significantly smaller than one point five billion.
He looked at it for one second and felt the familiar brief ache of watching wealth become resources.
Then he let it go, because everything he’d spent had a face attached to it and a reason that mattered, and that was the correct way for causality to be used.
One item remained.
He scrolled to it and felt something settle in him — not excitement exactly, more the quiet recognition of something that had been a long time coming finally being within reach.
Cradle Seed of Elements (Mythical – Item)
Once planted in the body, it gradually enhances all elemental affinities.
Vendor: Keeper of The Dimension
He looked at it for a moment.

Not hesitating. Just sitting with it — the item he’d been watching since he first found it in the shop, calculated toward, been too short of causality for through every battle and every clear until today.
He pressed buy.
The golden screen flickered once.
The air in front of him bent slightly at the edges, reality folding in the specific way it did when the cosmic shop delivered something physical, and the Cradle Seed of Elements began to materialize.
On the rock twenty meters ahead of him, Vyra’s fire burned brighter.

chapters.title: Chapter 546: Preparations Before the Awakening Dungeon—2
paragraphs: The Cradle Seed of Elements materialized in front of him, and Leon stared at it.

Not a seed. Not even close to a seed. The name had built an expectation that the object would immediately be demolished — what floated before him was closer to an orb, crystalline, roughly the size of his closed fist, cycling through every color he could name and several he didn’t have names for in a slow, continuous shift with no pattern and no repetition.

Deep violet bleeding into gold, ocean-blue threading through something that existed more as the impression of a color than the color itself, greens and reds and whites and blacks all present simultaneously without any of them canceling the others out.

He’d seen something like this before. The memory arrived without effort — the Orb of All Elemental Affinity, the object that had started everything, the thing that had given him access to every elemental affinity and produced the SSS-ranked class that had defined his entire path since. The Cradle Seed carried that same quality of containing too many things at once without any of them competing.

The attraction hit him the moment it fully materialized. Not metaphorical — physical, something in his body leaning toward the object before his mind had formed a conscious response. And then, inexplicably, his mouth watered.

He stared at the crystalline orb, and his body was treating it like food. Like something it needed in a specific way, the body communicated a genuine need rather than a simple preference. There was no instruction manual, no additional system description beyond what the shop listing had shown him. Just the object, present and radiating something that his Primordial Void Heart was apparently interpreting as exactly what it had been waiting for.
Absorb it now or wait for the dungeon.
He thought it through properly rather than letting the pull make the decision for him.

The dungeon was the uncertainty. His class — SSS-ranked, Elemental Paragon, a designation he’d never encountered on anyone else — might sit outside whatever classification system the dungeon used for entry. If the dungeon turned out to be incompatible with his class, or if the scaling simply didn’t apply to something at his level, he’d have delayed for nothing.

But the other side of the argument was stronger. The Cradle Seed enhanced all elemental affinities — the foundation of essentially everything he did in combat. Absorbing it before the dungeon meant whatever transformation it produced would already be integrated by the time he entered. His performance inside would reflect the improved foundation rather than the pre-improvement one. If the dungeon did accept him, he’d be going in stronger.
And if it didn’t — his world was rank three. More class-reawakening dungeons would form. This wasn’t the last opportunity. Only the timing was unique, not the opportunity itself.
Six days,he calculated. Fifteen-day window, nine elapsed. Six remaining, possibly fewer depending on how the dungeon’s opening timeline played out.
He could absorb a mythical item in six days. He was reasonably confident of that.
The decision was settled.

He pulled out a storage ring and transferred everything — equipment for Seraphine, Ira, Vyra, and Loriel, the bulk artifacts for the dungeon participants, all four thousand two hundred potions, every piece of preparation he’d just spent the past hour purchasing — from his soul-connected inventory into the ring. Then, with a single directed thought, he sent the ring across the dimensional world to where his clone was overseeing the new city’s development.

No message needed. Same mind. The clone received it and understood the complete context simultaneously — the distribution plan, the lending conditions, every detail — without a single word passing between them.
If he didn’t make it back before the dungeon opened, the clone would handle everything. He wasn’t worried. But he intended to finish long before that became relevant.
He checked on Vyra before leaving.

The fire around her had changed quality — the complex cycling patterns of deep transformation had simplified into something more settled, more present, the movement of fire that had finished becoming something rather than fire in the process of becoming it. Whatever the transition from level four to level five Aura actually looked like from the inside, he’d just watched the outside of it resolve.
She opened her eyes.

They looked at each other across twenty meters of mountain rock. Leon gave her a single nod. She returned it, and he teleported before the moment extended into a conversation, because she clearly had things to say and he didn’t have time to receive them right now.
He chose his location deliberately.

One kilometer from the tower. He placed himself with awareness of the distances — the tower behind him, Xyra’s mansion visible just beyond it, the specific geometry of the site chosen rather than arrived at randomly.

He hadn’t gone to her to announce what he was doing. He’d considered it and decided against it. She would come if something went wrong — would feel it through her connection to the world and arrive regardless of whether he’d warned her — but going to her first meant a conversation, and conversations with Xyra had a demonstrated tendency to develop in directions he hadn’t planned for and couldn’t always extract himself from on his own timeline.

He thought about her for a moment with the particular mix of feelings she reliably produced. Ancient, unfathomable, possessed of a beauty that made the word inadequate, and somehow also exactly the kind of person who had apparently decided he was her primary focus now that she had a physical body and no remaining constraints on expressing that focus. The inexperience underneath all the power — the specific inexperience of someone who had watched the world from behind glass for hundreds of thousands of years and was now encountering the actual texture of it for the first time.
He found it more endearing than he’d expected to find it. That was a fact he was choosing not to examine too closely.
She’d come if he needed her. That was enough for now.
He sat down cross-legged on the rock, spine straight, and got serious about preparation.

Two revival treasures were equipped — the best ones remaining in his personal stock after the distribution. Healing potion within immediate reach. Mana potion beside it. He wasn’t going into a mythical item absorption without a safety net, regardless of how confident he felt about the outcome.

He looked at the space around him — open rock, good sightlines, nothing nearby that could be damaged by whatever the Cradle Seed produced during absorption. He’d chosen the location for Xyra’s proximity and for the clear space equally.
He reached into his soul-connected inventory.
The Cradle Seed came out warm in his palm, the color-cycling slowing slightly as he held it directly, as though it recognized the contact and was taking its time to orient toward him specifically.
He looked at it for one more moment — the shifting colors, the warmth coming off it, the pull that his body had been producing since it first appeared.
He took a breath.
Put it in his mouth.
Swallowed.

The taste was beyond his vocabulary — every flavor simultaneously, which produced something that was none of them, moving down his throat with a warmth that became heat by the time it reached his chest and then something beyond heat entirely as it found the Primordial Void Heart and the Void Heart responded.
THUMMM.

The pulse was different from the slow, heavy rhythm he knew. Deeper. The heart recognized the Cradle Seed as something that belonged inside him, something that had been designed for exactly this — to be planted, as the listing had said, and to grow.
Every elemental affinity lit up simultaneously.

Not painful. Intense — the specific feeling of something expanding at speed, all affinities responding at once to the Cradle Seed beginning to distribute itself through his system. Space, lightning, light, fire, wind, ice, life, holy — he could feel each one of them individually and all of them together, the Cradle Seed moving through the pathways between them like water finding every channel available.

He kept his breathing even. His eyes stayed open. He was monitoring the process rather than simply experiencing it, the analytical part of him staying functional even as the physical intensity climbed.

The warmth from the Cradle Seed and the heat from his Void Heart’s response were building toward something — a convergence point he could feel approaching without being able to predict the shape of what would happen when they met.
He was ready for it to be demanding.
He was braced for it to take time.
Then the fluctuation happened directly in front of him.

The air rippled — not the clean silver-white of his own spatial work, not the deliberate geometry of the tower’s passages, not anything he recognized from his own toolkit or from anything he’d encountered before. A disturbance in the space directly before him, unplanned, arriving from somewhere rather than opening to somewhere, with a quality his spatial awareness reached toward and couldn’t immediately classify.
Leon stared at it, the Cradle Seed’s heat still moving through him, and felt genuine uncertainty for the first time in a while.

chapters.title: Chapter 547: Cradle Seed of Element.
paragraphs: The figure that materialized from the spatial fluctuation was Xyra.
Leon looked up at her from his cross-legged position, the Cradle Seed’s warmth already moving through his chest, and read her face.

Something was different. Not the usual amusement, not the particular directness she’d been deploying since getting her body back. Something quieter and considerably more serious sat on her expression, her silver eyes fixed on him with an attention that felt like monitoring rather than watching.
She came here for a reason,he thought.And it isn’t a social call.
He kept his breathing even and said nothing, reading her for information while the warmth of the Cradle Seed continued its work through every elemental pathway simultaneously.
Xyra had been watching him since he left the tower.

Not stalking. The concept was beneath her and faintly offensive to consider. She was the spirit of this world — everything that moved within it was available to her awareness if she chose to look. She had simply chosen to look at him specifically because she was bored, and because her mana recovery was slow enough that sitting with her own thoughts was not particularly entertaining.

The recovery was going to take months. Possibly a year. Even as a rank-three world, the ambient mana here was genuinely thin by her standards — insufficient for a being of her caliber in a way that would have been insulting if she’d had the energy to be insulted by it. Her new body was subpar. Functional, present, real in the ways that mattered, but sluggish in terms of mana control and considerably more fragile than what she was accustomed to working with.

Her original body sat in its cage somewhere in this world, intact and perfectly preserved. She wasn’t worried about it — she was a Prime Divinity, and her original body even without her soul attached to it.
A million years could pass, and the result would be a body that was slightly stiff. Nothing more. What she could do now, slowly, was work on breaking through the cage from the outside.

That was possible, if extremely slow — hundreds of years at minimum, given the constraints. Breaking through from the inside had never been possible at all. The cage had been built specifically to prevent that. Outside was always the only option, and outside simply took time.
She watched Leon because watching him was more interesting than the alternative.

She’d already known about his cosmic system access — had observed him using it multiple times and felt no particular shock about it. She understood how that access was granted. SS and SSS-ranked classes — genuine geniuses of the universe, recognized by the cosmic system’s own will — received it regardless of cultivation rank or world of origin. The system itself had a will of its own, and it had chosen to acknowledge him. That told her something without her needing to ask.

She didn’t know if his class was SS or SSS. She’d never asked directly. But from what she’d observed — the quality of what he deployed, the way he operated — her guess was SSS with confidence. The difference between class ranks wasn’t immediately obvious at low cultivation levels, only a few times stronger at the start. But at higher ranks, the gap became something else entirely, impossibly vast, the kind of difference that made comparison feel meaningless.
Nine affinities. All of them rank seven. Time, space, lightning, wind, water, fire, dark, life, light — she’d cataloged them through observation and through direct contact.
It was her mouth,she thought,but contact was contact. That was enough to confirm rank seven across all nine.

The most impressive person she’d encountered previously in terms of affinity had carried ten — one more than Leon appeared to have. But of those ten, only two were rank seven, one was rank eight, and the rest sat at around ranks four, five, and six, with only one rare affinity among them.
Leon, with five rare affinities all at rank seven, was thousands of times more impressive than that person by any reasonable accounting.

What she didn’t know — what her observation couldn’t reach — was that nine was not the actual number. Nine were simply the affinities he’d deployed where she could observe them. He possessed all elemental affinities, every single one, each at rank seven, held in such perfect harmony and kept so thoroughly contained that even her direct physical contact hadn’t been enough to detect the full scope of it. Unless he chose to show her, she would never know.
She would have needed significant time to process that information.
She’d seen him find the Cradle Seed in the cosmic shop. Had watched the listing resolve on his screen and recognized it immediately.
Two things hit her at once.

First — fury. The Keeper of the Dimension. The same entity that had locked her away for hundreds of thousands of years was now selling something that had once been hers. At seven hundred and ninety million casualties, which was a price that made her genuinely angry, not because it was expensive but because it wascheap. Three or four times that number would have barely scratched the actual value. The Keeper had stolen it from her and was now selling it for a fraction of what it was worth.
Second — doubt. Because the Keeper had stolen it from her, and she didn’t know what the Keeper had done to it since, and she couldn’t verify from observation whether it actually worked.
Only if it actually fucking worked,she thought.

Here was the reality that most people didn’t understand about affinity treasures: almost none of them worked. The market was flooded with items claiming to grant new affinities or elevate existing ones, and their stated success rates were lies constructed through careful selection of compatible buyers.

The real success rate for a random person attempting to use one of these treasures was one in a million. The advertised rate looked better only because sellers made sure to sell exclusively to people who already had a natural near-compatibility, making their treasure appear functional when it was simply matching people who would have succeeded regardless.
Above rank six, genuine affinity improvement treasures essentially didn’t exist. Nothing on the market reliably worked at that level.

She had even been slightly shocked when she’d watched the purple-haired woman — Seraphine — absorb the Stormlight Seed that the hag was selling. She’d thought it was nearly a scam from the start. Seraphine had possessed a single affinity: lightning. Only lightning. And somehow she had absorbed the Stormlight Seed successfully, gained the rare light affinity from nothing, and had her lightning affinity upgraded in the process. The number of people across the universe who would have wanted to do exactly that and had failed — and who would have puked blood hearing that someone with only a single starting affinity managed it — was enormous. Almost ninety-five percent of the universe, Xyra estimated, would have lost their composure completely upon learning of this outcome.

She had blamed it on his luck. Leon’s luck, specifically, because the impossible things that happened around him were too consistent to be random. The universe had given him too much, this little devil, and somehow the luck extended to the people around him as well.
Which meant, potentially, the Cradle Seed might work for him when it would fail for anyone else.
Or it might not work at all. Or it might work in a way that the misfortune recorded in the ancient texts was describing.
She had not intervened when he bought it. Curiosity and the recognition that the luck was real kept her still.
Then he put it in his mouth and swallowed it.
I messed up,she thought, and materialized immediately.

She hadn’t spent significant mana arriving here — she was the spirit of this world; movement within it required almost nothing from her. But what she was worried about spending was something far more significant. If something went wrong with the absorption, which was even known if you had swallowed it or not, whether it was the correct way or not, stabilizing it would require her mana reserves and potentially her soul force — the deep reserve that didn’t recover quickly and whose expenditure left permanent marks on a being’s existence.

She could not pull the Cradle Seed out of him by force. Even if the physical extraction were possible without tearing his elemental pathways apart, introducing an external force into an active absorption was the kind of intervention that made outcomes worse. She knew this.

She couldn’t interfere with the Cradle Seed’s process through time manipulation either — something at its actual classification level would produce backlash, and the backlash, combined with whatever was already happening, could be catastrophic.
What she could do was be here. Soul force in reserve, ready.

The misfortune record sat in her memory with a weight it hadn’t had before Leon swallowed the thing. Ancient texts around the Cradle Seed consistently noted misfortune following it, one of which was the same scenario: no result known, but she can imagine it — seeing this thing being here. Most of the misfortune she initially attributed to the greed of those who pursued it. She was a Prime Divinity. The universe arranged things in her favor. The Cradle Seed in her possession had not brought misfortune to her.
But she had not swallowed it. And the record referenced someone who had.

Even other Prime Divinities and so-called gods — beings with the knowledge and power to make informed choices about ancient treasures with ominous reputations attached — would not have casually swallowed something like this. The promise of power didn’t override the warning. That was simply not how beings of that level operated.
Leon had swallowed it like it was a meal.
She stood two meters in front of him, soul force ready, mana on standby, watching him breathe steadily with his eyes closed and his face completely still, and blamed herself for not moving faster.
He was completely unaware of any of this.
