chapters.title: Chapter 550: Training
paragraphs: Leon teleported to an empty glass field.

The landscape was strange in a specific way; certain parts of his dimensional world were strange — flat, crystalline ground that caught the ambient light and scattered it in directions that didn’t quite follow normal physics, stretching in every direction without feature or interruption.
Nobody came here. He’d chosen it precisely for that reason.
He had found this reason through his clone, which had decided to travel far ahead of the grassy region, and he had found this.
He needed space, and he needed privacy, and he needed nobody to accidentally walk into whatever he was about to do.

He wasn’t going to Seraphine or the others. They were training, and he wasn’t going to be the reason they stopped. The treasure distribution was already handled — he’d confirmed it through the shared awareness with his clone without needing to send a message or open a portal. Same mind, same information, no communication required.
The first thing he did was open his status screen and check the affinity line.
[Affinity: All Elemental (Rank 7+??)]
He stared at the plus sign and the question marks for a moment.

Not rank eight. But not rank seven either — something above seven and below eight that the system apparently didn’t have clean language for, the plus sign and the trailing question marks the closest it could get to describing a threshold state it hadn’t been designed to accommodate. He didn’t need the status screen to tell him this. He could feel it already, the difference present and unmistakable, every affinity responding with a closeness and clarity it hadn’t had before the absorption.

The question marks bothered him slightly. Not because they were alarming — because they suggested the system itself wasn’t certain what to make of what he was carrying, which raised questions about what the Cradle Seed had actually done versus what it was supposed to do.
He closed the screen and sent a thought outward.

Xyra. A simple request — he wanted the time ratio in this area increased. One thousand times faster than outside. A hundred times faster than the standard ten-to-one his dimensional world normally ran at.
The change happened before he’d finished forming the thought completely.

He felt it through his time affinity — just barely, the detection only possible because he’d been expecting it and because the affinity’s sensitivity had increased enough after the absorption to register what it previously couldn’t. Time shifted around him, the area of glass field contracting into its own accelerated bubble while the rest of the world continued at its normal pace outside it.
She’s useful,he thought, with genuine appreciation.Genuinely, consistently useful.

A separate thought surfaced briefly — the red dragon, still in its coma state on the isolated mountain. His clone checked on it regularly. Vyra visited. Xyra had already looked into it after he’d brought it through the portal, and her assessment had been clear: leave it alone. Interference with a being in that specific mental state could cause damage that natural recovery wouldn’t. The dragon’s body was absorbing ambient mana continuously, sustaining itself, healing at whatever pace its own nature permitted. It would wake when it was ready.
He’d taken her advice seriously and hadn’t pushed it further.
He set that thought aside and turned his attention to what he was here for.
He started with fire.

Not because it was his strongest affinity or the one he was most comfortable with — because fire was honest. Fire showed you exactly what it was doing at every moment. There was no ambiguity in whether the fire element was responding to your intent or running on its own momentum. He could use that clarity to measure what had changed.
He extended his fire affinity outward and called a flame into existence above his open palm.
The flame that appeared was not what he expected.

It was larger than his intent had specified. Denser, the color deeper — not the orange-yellow of standard fire element but something closer to white at the core, the heat radiating from it measurably greater than what the visual scale suggested. He hadn’t pushed it. He’d simply called it the way he had ten thousand times before.
The response was different in kind, not just degree.
Rank 7+,he thought, watching the flame rotate slowly above his hand.Whatever that plus sign means, this is what it means in practice.

He pushed the flame higher. It went without resistance, scaling with his intent in a way that felt frictionless, the element not fighting his control but moving with it. He pulled it back, and it compressed cleanly, density increasing rather than dissipating.
He let it go, and it dissolved into the air without residue.

He moved to lightning next. Then the wind. Then ice — his most developed aura-type affinity, the one closest to the transition he was working toward. Then light, then darkness, then life, then space, then time.

Each one showed the same quality. Not dramatically different in power output at the surface level — he wasn’t doing anything extraordinary with any of them, just calling them and shaping them and releasing them. But the response. The relationship between intent and result. The absence of resistance that had previously existed in a thin but perceptible layer between what he wanted and what the element did.
That layer was gone.
Or not gone — compressed below the threshold of detection, made functionally irrelevant by the affinity’s increased sensitivity to him specifically.

He spent time with each one. Not practicing techniques — just listening, the way you listened to a piece of music you knew well that someone had suddenly played in a different key. The same structure, different quality.
Then he turned to the ice aura.

He’d watched Vyra make the transition from level four to level five during her training on the mountain. Had observed it from outside without seeing the internal experience of it, the process only visible through its external effects — the fire that changed quality, the specific settling of something that had finished becoming rather than being in the process of it.

He had rank four in both ice and lightning aura. Ice was more developed — had been for a while, for reasons he’d never fully examined but that he suspected had something to do with the specific way he’d developed his spatial affinity alongside it, the two elements having a certain complementary quality in how he used them.
He activated it now and felt the familiar crystalline layer extend across his body, the ice aura’s characteristic quality of making the air around him feel colder and denser simultaneously.
Then he pushed past the familiar.

Not toward a specific technique or application. Toward understanding — the thing Xyra had said about level five aura that he hadn’t fully unpacked until watching her achieve it. Level five wasn’t like level four. Level five was what happened when comprehension of the element went deep enough that the distinction between the element and the person using it became genuinely unclear.
He pushed the ice aura’s comprehension downward into the element itself, not upward into application.
The glass field around him began to frost.

Not from his intent directly — from the aura radiating naturally, the element responding to his deepening engagement with it by participating rather than waiting. The frost spread in patterns across the crystalline ground, following the grain of the material the way frost followed the texture of glass in cold air, except the temperature hadn’t dropped enough for this to happen naturally.
The element was meeting him halfway.

He sat down cross-legged in the middle of it and kept pushing, the 1000x time flowing around him, the crystalline field frosting steadily outward from where he sat, and lost track of everything except the depth he was trying to reach.
